x: move zeroes to left movezeroestoleft.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easyarrays; import java.util.arrays; /** * problem: move all zeroes in an array to the left end, while keeping the * relative order of the non-zero elements. * * example: * input: [1, 0, 0, 7, 8] * output: [0, 0, 1, 7, 8] */ public class movezeroestoleft { /** * approach 1: copy into a new array, filling from the right. * * idea: same as move-zeroes-right, but we walk the input backwards and * place non-zero values starting from the last slot of the result. */ public static int[] usingextraarray(int[] nums) { int[] result = new int[nums.length]; // all zeroes by default int index = nums.length - 1; // next free slot, from the right for (int i = nums.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) { if (nums[i] != 0) { result[index] = nums[i]; index--; } } // the untouched front of result already contains the zeroes. return result; } /** * approach 2: two pointers, reusing the same array. * * idea: "insertpos" starts at the last index and marks where the next * non-zero value (found while scanning backwards) should go. once the * scan finishes, everything from index 0 up to insertpos becomes 0. */ public static void usingtwopointers(int[] nums) { int insertpos = nums.length - 1; // next position for a non-zero value // pass 1: compact all non-zero values to the back (order preserved). for (int i = nums.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) { if (nums[i] != 0) { nums[insertpos] = nums[i]; insertpos--; } } // pass 2: fill the remaining front with zeroes. while (insertpos >= 0) { nums[insertpos] = 0; insertpos--; } } public static void main(string[] args) { int[] input = { 1, 0, 0, 7, 8 }; system.out.println("input: " + arrays.tostring(input)); system.out.println("extra array: " + arrays.tostring(usingextraarray(input))); int[] inplace = input.clone(); // clone so both demos see the same input usingtwopointers(inplace); system.out.println("two pointers: " + arrays.tostring(inplace)); } }

s: Move all zeroes in an array to the right end, while keeping the relative order of the non-zero elements.
x: move zeroes to right movezeroestoright.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easyarrays; import java.util.arrays; /** * problem: move all zeroes in an array to the right end, while keeping the * relative order of the non-zero elements. * * example: * input: [1, 0, 0, 2, 4, 5, 0, 0] * output: [1, 2, 4, 5, 0, 0, 0, 0] */ public class movezeroestoright { /** * approach 1: copy into a new array (simplest to write). * * idea: copy every non-zero value into a fresh array, left to right. * a new int[] is already filled with 0s, so the trailing zeroes come * for free. */ public static int[] usingextraarray(int[] nums) { int[] result = new int[nums.length]; // all zeroes by default int index = 0; // next free slot in result for (int num : nums) { if (num != 0) { result[index] = num; index++; } } // nothing to fill at the end: result was born zero-filled. return result; } /** * approach 2: two pointers, reusing the same array. * * idea: "insertpos" marks where the next non-zero value should go. * scan left to right; every non-zero value is placed at insertpos and * insertpos moves forward. after the scan, everything from insertpos * to the end becomes 0. */ public static void usingtwopointers(int[] nums) { int insertpos = 0; // next position reserved for a non-zero value // pass 1: compact all non-zero values to the front (order preserved). for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) { if (nums[i] != 0) { nums[insertpos] = nums[i]; insertpos++; } } // pass 2: fill the remaining tail with zeroes. while (insertpos < nums.length) { nums[insertpos] = 0; insertpos++; } } public static void main(string[] args) { int[] input = { 1, 0, 0, 2, 4, 5, 0, 0 }; system.out.println("input: " + arrays.tostring(input)); system.out.println("extra array: " + arrays.tostring(usingextraarray(input))); int[] inplace = input.clone(); // clone so both demos see the same input usingtwopointers(inplace); system.out.println("two pointers: " + arrays.tostring(inplace)); } }

s: Remove duplicate values from an array so each value appears only once.
x: remove duplicates from array removeduplicatesfromarray.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easyarrays; import java.util.arrays; import java.util.linkedhashset; import java.util.set; /** * problem: remove duplicate values from an array so each value appears * only once. * * example: * input: [1, 3, 3, 4, 4, 7, 7, 7] * output: [1, 3, 4, 7] * * which approach fits depends on the input: use the set approach for * unsorted input; the two-pointer approach only works on sorted input. */ public class removeduplicatesfromarray { /** * approach 1: linkedhashset (simplest — shows you know collections). * * idea: a set stores each value only once, so adding everything and * reading the set back removes duplicates for free. linkedhashset * (not plain hashset) preserves first-seen order — choose it * deliberately and say why. */ public static int[] usinglinkedhashset(int[] nums) { set<integer> unique = new linkedhashset<>(); for (int num : nums) { unique.add(num); // duplicates are ignored by the set } // convert the set back to an int[] for the caller. int[] result = new int[unique.size()]; int i = 0; for (int num : unique) { result[i] = num; i++; } return result; } /** * approach 2: two pointers, reusing the array — requires sorted input. * * idea: in a sorted array, duplicates are always adjacent. "writepos" * tracks where the next new value goes; the scan pointer looks for * values different from the previous one. * returns the new length; elements beyond it are stale leftovers. */ public static int usingtwopointersonsorted(int[] sortednums) { if (sortednums.length == 0) { return 0; } int writepos = 1; // slot for the next distinct value (index 0 is kept) for (int scan = 1; scan < sortednums.length; scan++) { // a value different from the previous one is definitely new // (only valid because the array is sorted). if (sortednums[scan] != sortednums[scan - 1]) { sortednums[writepos] = sortednums[scan]; writepos++; } } return writepos; // logical new length } public static void main(string[] args) { int[] input = { 1, 3, 3, 4, 4, 7, 7, 7 }; system.out.println("input: " + arrays.tostring(input)); system.out.println("linkedhashset: " + arrays.tostring(usinglinkedhashset(input))); int[] sorted = input.clone(); arrays.sort(sorted); int newlength = usingtwopointersonsorted(sorted); // only the first newlength slots are meaningful after the in-place pass. system.out.println("two pointers: " + arrays.tostring(arrays.copyof(sorted, newlength))); } }

s: Find the second largest DISTINCT number in an array.
x: second largest number secondlargestnumber.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easyarrays; import java.util.arrays; /** * problem: find the second largest distinct number in an array. * * examples: * [1, 4, 7, 8, 2] -> 7 * [8, 8, 7] -> 7 (duplicates of the max don't count) * [5, 5, 5] -> no answer (only one distinct value) * * when there is no answer (fewer than 2 elements, or all values equal), * these methods throw illegalargumentexception; returning -1 is also a * common convention. */ public class secondlargestnumber { /** * approach 1: sort, then walk down from the top (simple to write). * * idea: after sorting, the largest value sits at the end. walk * backwards and return the first value strictly smaller than it — * that is the second largest distinct value. * we clone before sorting so the caller's array is not mutated. */ public static int usingsorting(int[] nums) { if (nums.length < 2) { throw new illegalargumentexception("need at least 2 elements"); } int[] sorted = nums.clone(); arrays.sort(sorted); int largest = sorted[sorted.length - 1]; for (int i = sorted.length - 2; i >= 0; i--) { if (sorted[i] != largest) { return sorted[i]; // first smaller value from the top } } throw new illegalargumentexception("no distinct second largest exists"); } /** * approach 2: single pass with two trackers (the neat answer). * * idea: carry two values through the array: * largest — biggest value seen so far * secondlargest — biggest value seen that is not "largest" * when a new max appears, the old max is demoted to secondlargest. */ public static int usingsinglepass(int[] nums) { if (nums.length < 2) { throw new illegalargumentexception("need at least 2 elements"); } int largest = integer.min_value; int secondlargest = integer.min_value; for (int num : nums) { if (num > largest) { secondlargest = largest; // old max becomes the runner-up largest = num; } else if (num > secondlargest && num != largest) { // between second and max, and not a duplicate of the max. secondlargest = num; } } if (secondlargest == integer.min_value) { throw new illegalargumentexception("no distinct second largest exists"); } return secondlargest; } public static void main(string[] args) { int[] input = { 1, 4, 7, 8, 2 }; system.out.println("sorting: " + usingsorting(input)); system.out.println("single pass: " + usingsinglepass(input)); int[] withduplicates = { 8, 8, 7 }; system.out.println("duplicates case [8, 8, 7]: " + usingsinglepass(withduplicates)); } }

s: Find the second smallest DISTINCT number in an array.
x: second smallest number secondsmallestnumber.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easyarrays; import java.util.arrays; /** * problem: find the second smallest distinct number in an array. * * examples: * [4, 1, 2, 1, 3] -> 2 (duplicates of the minimum don't count) * [7, 7, 7] -> no answer (only one distinct value) * * mirror image of secondlargestnumber — same two patterns, flipped. * when there is no answer (fewer than 2 elements, or all values equal), * these methods throw illegalargumentexception. */ public class secondsmallestnumber { /** * approach 1: sort, then walk up from the bottom. * * idea: after an ascending sort, the smallest value sits at index 0. * walk forward and return the first value strictly bigger than it — * that is the second smallest distinct value. we clone before * sorting so the caller's array is not mutated. */ public static int usingsorting(int[] nums) { if (nums.length < 2) { throw new illegalargumentexception("need at least 2 elements"); } int[] sorted = nums.clone(); arrays.sort(sorted); int smallest = sorted[0]; for (int i = 1; i < sorted.length; i++) { if (sorted[i] != smallest) { return sorted[i]; // first bigger value from the bottom } } throw new illegalargumentexception("no distinct second smallest exists"); } /** * approach 2: single pass with two trackers. * * idea: carry two values through the array: * smallest — smallest value seen so far * secondsmallest — smallest value seen that is not "smallest" * when a new minimum appears, the old minimum is promoted to * secondsmallest. */ public static int usingsinglepass(int[] nums) { if (nums.length < 2) { throw new illegalargumentexception("need at least 2 elements"); } int smallest = integer.max_value; int secondsmallest = integer.max_value; for (int num : nums) { if (num < smallest) { secondsmallest = smallest; // old minimum becomes the runner-up smallest = num; } else if (num < secondsmallest && num != smallest) { // above the minimum, and not a duplicate of it. secondsmallest = num; } } if (secondsmallest == integer.max_value) { throw new illegalargumentexception("no distinct second smallest exists"); } return secondsmallest; } public static void main(string[] args) { int[] input = { 4, 1, 2, 1, 3 }; system.out.println("sorting: " + usingsorting(input)); system.out.println("single pass: " + usingsinglepass(input)); int[] withduplicates = { 1, 1, 5 }; system.out.println("duplicates case [1, 1, 5]: " + usingsinglepass(withduplicates)); } }

s: Find the smallest number in an array.
x: smallest number smallestnumber.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easyarrays; import java.util.arrays; /** * problem: find the smallest number in an array. * * example: * input: [2, 98, 3, 1, 6, 8] * output: 1 * * this is the mirror image of largestnumber — same patterns, flipped * comparisons. */ public class smallestnumber { /** * approach 1: loop with a running champion. * * idea: keep the smallest value seen so far. mirror of the largest * version: initialize to integer.max_value (not 0!) so the champion * always loses to the first real element, even on all-positive or * all-negative arrays. */ public static int usingloop(int[] nums) { int smallest = integer.max_value; for (int num : nums) { if (num < smallest) { smallest = num; } } return smallest; } /** * approach 2: sort and take the first element. * * idea: after an ascending sort, the smallest value sits in slot 0. * we clone first so the caller's array is not reordered. */ public static int usingsorting(int[] nums) { int[] sorted = nums.clone(); arrays.sort(sorted); return sorted[0]; } /** * approach 3: java 8 streams. * * idea: same stream as the largest version, with min() instead of * max(). */ public static int usingstreams(int[] nums) { return arrays.stream(nums) .min() .orelsethrow(); } public static void main(string[] args) { int[] input = { 2, 98, 3, 1, 6, 8 }; system.out.println("loop: " + usingloop(input)); system.out.println("sorting: " + usingsorting(input)); system.out.println("streams: " + usingstreams(input)); } }

s: Sort an array in ascending order using built-in tools.
x: sort an array sortanarray.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easyarrays; import java.util.arrays; import java.util.collections; /** * problem: sort an array in ascending order using built-in tools. * * example: * input: [4, 3, 4, 4, 5, 9, 7, 8] * output: [3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9] * * for the hand-written version (bubble sort), see bubblesort in this * package — this file is about knowing what the standard library gives * you for free. */ public class sortanarray { /** * approach 1: arrays.sort (the standard answer). * * idea: arrays.sort(int[]) sorts the array in place — there is no * return value; the array you pass in comes back sorted. we clone * the input first so the original order is preserved for the other * demos. */ public static int[] usingarrayssort(int[] nums) { int[] sorted = nums.clone(); arrays.sort(sorted); return sorted; } /** * approach 2: descending order with collections.reverseorder(). * * idea: arrays.sort can take a comparator (an object that decides * which of two values comes first), and collections.reverseorder() * is the ready-made "biggest first" comparator. catch: comparators * only work on objects, so the int[] must be boxed into integer[] * first — boxing means wrapping each primitive int in an integer * object. */ public static integer[] usingdescending(int[] nums) { integer[] boxed = arrays.stream(nums).boxed().toarray(integer[]::new); arrays.sort(boxed, collections.reverseorder()); return boxed; } /** * approach 3: java 8 streams. * * idea: stream the array, let sorted() order it, and collect back * with toarray(). streams never mutate the source, so no clone * needed. */ public static int[] usingstreams(int[] nums) { return arrays.stream(nums) .sorted() .toarray(); } public static void main(string[] args) { int[] input = { 4, 3, 4, 4, 5, 9, 7, 8 }; system.out.println("arrays.sort: " + arrays.tostring(usingarrayssort(input))); system.out.println("descending: " + arrays.tostring(usingdescending(input))); system.out.println("streams: " + arrays.tostring(usingstreams(input))); system.out.println("original untouched: " + arrays.tostring(input)); } }

s: Swap the values of two variables.
x: swap program swapprogram.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easyarrays; import java.util.arrays; /** * problem: swap the values of two variables. * * example: a = 10, b = 20 -> a = 20, b = 10 * * note: java passes arguments by value, so a void swap(a, b) method can * never change the caller's variables. that is why these methods return * the swapped pair instead. */ public class swapprogram { /** * approach 1: temp variable (the standard answer). * * idea: park "a" in temp so its value survives while we overwrite it. */ public static int[] usingtempvariable(int a, int b) { int temp = a; // save a a = b; // a takes b's value b = temp; // b takes the saved original a return new int[] { a, b }; } /** * approach 2: arithmetic, no third variable. * warning: a + b can overflow integer.max_value and corrupt the result. * * idea: store the sum in "a", then recover each original value by * subtracting the other. */ public static int[] usingarithmetic(int a, int b) { a = a + b; // a now holds (original a + original b) b = a - b; // sum - b = original a -> b is swapped a = a - b; // sum - original a = original b -> a is swapped return new int[] { a, b }; } /** * approach 3: xor, no third variable, no overflow. * * idea: relies on two bit facts — x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x. * values cancel out pairwise, leaving each variable with the other's * original value. */ public static int[] usingxor(int a, int b) { a = a ^ b; // a = a ^ b b = a ^ b; // b = (a ^ b) ^ b = a ^ (b ^ b) = a ^ 0 = original a a = a ^ b; // a = (a ^ b) ^ a = (a ^ a) ^ b = 0 ^ b = original b return new int[] { a, b }; } public static void main(string[] args) { int a = 10; int b = 20; system.out.println("before: a=" + a + " b=" + b); system.out.println("temp variable: " + arrays.tostring(usingtempvariable(a, b))); system.out.println("arithmetic: " + arrays.tostring(usingarithmetic(a, b))); system.out.println("xor: " + arrays.tostring(usingxor(a, b))); } }

import java.util.arrays; /** * problem: check whether two strings are anagrams — meaning they contain * exactly the same characters the same number of times, just rearranged. * * examples: * "silent" and "listen" -> true * "hello" and "world" -> false * * quick sanity check both approaches rely on: if the lengths differ, the * strings can never be anagrams, so we bail out early. */ public class anagram { /** * approach 1: sort both and compare (simplest to write). * * idea: anagrams are the same letters in a different order — so if we * sort the letters of both words, anagrams become identical strings. * arrays.sort() sorts a char[] in place, arrays.equals() compares two * arrays element by element. */ public static boolean usingsorting(string first, string second) { if (first.length() != second.length()) { return false; // different lengths -> can never be anagrams } char[] firstchars = first.tochararray(); char[] secondchars = second.tochararray(); arrays.sort(firstchars); arrays.sort(secondchars); return arrays.equals(firstchars, secondchars); } /** * approach 2: count letters up and back down. * * idea: use a small table with one slot per letter (a..z). walk the * first word adding +1 per letter, walk the second subtracting -1. * for true anagrams every slot ends back at exactly 0. * note: this table only covers lowercase a-z; for mixed-case or * punctuation, normalize first (tolowercase) or count with a hashmap. */ public static boolean usinglettercounts(string first, string second) { if (first.length() != second.length()) { return false; } int[] lettercounts = new int[26]; // one slot per letter, all start at 0 for (int i = 0; i < first.length(); i++) { lettercounts[first.charat(i) - 'a']++; // 'c' - 'a' = 2 -> slot for "c" lettercounts[second.charat(i) - 'a']--; } for (int count : lettercounts) { if (count != 0) { return false; // some letter appears a different number of times } } return true; } public static void main(string[] args) { system.out.println("silent / listen"); system.out.println(" sorting: " + usingsorting("silent", "listen")); system.out.println(" letter count: " + usinglettercounts("silent", "listen")); system.out.println("hello / world"); system.out.println(" sorting: " + usingsorting("hello", "world")); system.out.println(" letter count: " + usinglettercounts("hello", "world")); } } armstrong number check whether a number is an armstrong number — a number that equals the sum of its own digits, each raised to the power of the number of digits. armstrongnumber.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; /** * problem: check whether a number is an armstrong number — a number that * equals the sum of its own digits, each raised to the power of the * number of digits. * * examples: * 153 -> 1^3 + 5^3 + 3^3 = 1 + 125 + 27 = 153 -> true * 9474 -> 9^4 + 4^4 + 7^4 + 4^4 = 9474 -> true * 123 -> 1^3 + 2^3 + 3^3 = 36 -> false */ public class armstrongnumber { /** * approach 1: count digits with math, then sum the powers. * * idea: two passes with the % 10 / / 10 digit-peeling pair. pass 1 * counts how many digits there are; pass 2 adds up each digit raised * to that count. math.pow() returns a double, so we cast back to * int — fine here because the values involved are small and exact. */ public static boolean usingmath(int num) { int digits = 0; for (int temp = num; temp != 0; temp /= 10) { digits++; } int sum = 0; for (int temp = num; temp != 0; temp /= 10) { int digit = temp % 10; sum += (int) math.pow(digit, digits); // math.pow gives double -> cast } return sum == num; } /** * approach 2: count digits via the string form. * * idea: identical power-sum logic, but the digit count comes from * string.valueof(num).length() instead of a counting loop. handy * when you find string conversion easier to read than a temp loop. */ public static boolean usingstringlength(int num) { int digits = string.valueof(num).length(); int sum = 0; for (int temp = num; temp != 0; temp /= 10) { int digit = temp % 10; sum += (int) math.pow(digit, digits); } return sum == num; } public static void main(string[] args) { int[] samples = { 153, 9474, 123 }; for (int n : samples) { system.out.println(n + ": math -> " + usingmath(n) + ", string length -> " + usingstringlength(n)); } } } count character frequency count how many times each character appears in a string (character frequency). as a bonus, group characters by their frequency. countcharacterfrequency.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; import java.util.arraylist; import java.util.linkedhashmap; import java.util.list; import java.util.map; /** * problem: count how many times each character appears in a string * (character frequency). as a bonus, group characters by their frequency. * * example for "programming": * frequency: p=1, r=2, o=1, g=2, a=1, m=2, i=1, n=1 * grouped: 1=[p, o, a, i, n], 2=[r, g, m] * * java terms worth learning here: * - hashmap stores key -> value pairs; here character -> its count. * - linkedhashmap is a hashmap that remembers insertion order, so the * output lists characters in the order they first appeared. * - map.entry is one key-value pair inside a map; entryset() lets you * loop over all of them. */ public class countcharacterfrequency { /** * approach 1: nested loops — no map at all. * * idea: for each position, first check whether the character already * appeared earlier (inner loop over the positions before it). if it * did, skip — it was already reported. otherwise count its * occurrences by scanning forward. pure loops, no collections. */ public static void usingnestedloops(string text) { for (int i = 0; i < text.length(); i++) { char ch = text.charat(i); boolean seenearlier = false; for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) { if (text.charat(j) == ch) { seenearlier = true; break; } } if (seenearlier) { continue; // this character was already counted and printed } int count = 0; for (int j = i; j < text.length(); j++) { if (text.charat(j) == ch) { count++; } } system.out.println(ch + " -> " + count); } } /** * approach 2: the visited[] array technique — still no map. * * idea: same nested counting, but instead of re-scanning backwards * to check "seen earlier", we mark every matched position in a * parallel boolean array so the outer loop skips it later. this is * the classic "visited" pattern you will also see in * easyarrays.countarrayelement. */ public static void usingvisitedarray(string text) { char[] chars = text.tochararray(); boolean[] visited = new boolean[chars.length]; for (int i = 0; i < chars.length; i++) { if (visited[i]) { continue; // already counted inside an earlier group } int count = 1; for (int j = i + 1; j < chars.length; j++) { if (chars[i] == chars[j]) { count++; visited[j] = true; // don't recount this position later } } system.out.println(chars[i] + " -> " + count); } } /** * approach 3: hashmap with the classic containskey check. * * idea: for each character ask "have i counted you before?" if yes, * bump the stored count; if no, start it at 1. this is the verbose * version every java developer should be able to write from memory. */ public static map<character, integer> usingcontainskey(string text) { map<character, integer> frequency = new linkedhashmap<>(); for (char ch : text.tochararray()) { if (frequency.containskey(ch)) { frequency.put(ch, frequency.get(ch) + 1); // seen before -> add 1 } else { frequency.put(ch, 1); // first sighting -> start at 1 } } return frequency; } /** * approach 4: same idea, modern one-liner with merge() (java 8+). * * idea: map.merge(key, 1, integer::sum) means "store 1 if the key is * absent, otherwise add 1 to whatever is already there". one line * replaces the whole if/else — worth recognizing when you read other * people's code. */ public static map<character, integer> usingmerge(string text) { map<character, integer> frequency = new linkedhashmap<>(); for (char ch : text.tochararray()) { frequency.merge(ch, 1, integer::sum); } return frequency; } /** * bonus: flip the frequency map around — group characters by how many * times they appear. * * idea: build a new map of count -> list of characters with that * count. computeifabsent(count, k -> new arraylist<>()) creates the * list the first time a count appears, then we just add to it. */ public static map<integer, list<character>> groupbyfrequency(map<character, integer> frequency) { map<integer, list<character>> grouped = new linkedhashmap<>(); for (map.entry<character, integer> entry : frequency.entryset()) { char ch = entry.getkey(); int count = entry.getvalue(); grouped.computeifabsent(count, k -> new arraylist<>()).add(ch); } return grouped; } public static void main(string[] args) { string input = "programming"; system.out.println("nested loops (no map):"); usingnestedloops(input); system.out.println("visited array (no map):"); usingvisitedarray(input); system.out.println("containskey: " + usingcontainskey(input)); system.out.println("merge: " + usingmerge(input)); system.out.println("grouped: " + groupbyfrequency(usingmerge(input))); } } count specific character count how many times one specific character appears in a string. countspecificcharacter.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; s: Check whether two strings are ANAGRAMS — meaning they contain exactly the same characters the same number of times, just rearranged.
x: anagram anagram.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; import java.util.arrays; /** * problem: check whether two strings are anagrams — meaning they contain * exactly the same characters the same number of times, just rearranged. * * examples: * "silent" and "listen" -> true * "hello" and "world" -> false * * quick sanity check both approaches rely on: if the lengths differ, the * strings can never be anagrams, so we bail out early. */ public class anagram { /** * approach 1: sort both and compare (simplest to write). * * idea: anagrams are the same letters in a different order — so if we * sort the letters of both words, anagrams become identical strings. * arrays.sort() sorts a char[] in place, arrays.equals() compares two * arrays element by element. */ public static boolean usingsorting(string first, string second) { if (first.length() != second.length()) { return false; // different lengths -> can never be anagrams } char[] firstchars = first.tochararray(); char[] secondchars = second.tochararray(); arrays.sort(firstchars); arrays.sort(secondchars); return arrays.equals(firstchars, secondchars); } /** * approach 2: count letters up and back down. * * idea: use a small table with one slot per letter (a..z). walk the * first word adding +1 per letter, walk the second subtracting -1. * for true anagrams every slot ends back at exactly 0. * note: this table only covers lowercase a-z; for mixed-case or * punctuation, normalize first (tolowercase) or count with a hashmap. */ public static boolean usinglettercounts(string first, string second) { if (first.length() != second.length()) { return false; } int[] lettercounts = new int[26]; // one slot per letter, all start at 0 for (int i = 0; i < first.length(); i++) { lettercounts[first.charat(i) - 'a']++; // 'c' - 'a' = 2 -> slot for "c" lettercounts[second.charat(i) - 'a']--; } for (int count : lettercounts) { if (count != 0) { return false; // some letter appears a different number of times } } return true; } public static void main(string[] args) { system.out.println("silent / listen"); system.out.println(" sorting: " + usingsorting("silent", "listen")); system.out.println(" letter count: " + usinglettercounts("silent", "listen")); system.out.println("hello / world"); system.out.println(" sorting: " + usingsorting("hello", "world")); system.out.println(" letter count: " + usinglettercounts("hello", "world")); } }

s: Check whether a number is an ARMSTRONG NUMBER — a number that equals the sum of its own digits, each raised to the power of the number of digits.
x: armstrong number armstrongnumber.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; /** * problem: check whether a number is an armstrong number — a number that * equals the sum of its own digits, each raised to the power of the * number of digits. * * examples: * 153 -> 1^3 + 5^3 + 3^3 = 1 + 125 + 27 = 153 -> true * 9474 -> 9^4 + 4^4 + 7^4 + 4^4 = 9474 -> true * 123 -> 1^3 + 2^3 + 3^3 = 36 -> false */ public class armstrongnumber { /** * approach 1: count digits with math, then sum the powers. * * idea: two passes with the % 10 / / 10 digit-peeling pair. pass 1 * counts how many digits there are; pass 2 adds up each digit raised * to that count. math.pow() returns a double, so we cast back to * int — fine here because the values involved are small and exact. */ public static boolean usingmath(int num) { int digits = 0; for (int temp = num; temp != 0; temp /= 10) { digits++; } int sum = 0; for (int temp = num; temp != 0; temp /= 10) { int digit = temp % 10; sum += (int) math.pow(digit, digits); // math.pow gives double -> cast } return sum == num; } /** * approach 2: count digits via the string form. * * idea: identical power-sum logic, but the digit count comes from * string.valueof(num).length() instead of a counting loop. handy * when you find string conversion easier to read than a temp loop. */ public static boolean usingstringlength(int num) { int digits = string.valueof(num).length(); int sum = 0; for (int temp = num; temp != 0; temp /= 10) { int digit = temp % 10; sum += (int) math.pow(digit, digits); } return sum == num; } public static void main(string[] args) { int[] samples = { 153, 9474, 123 }; for (int n : samples) { system.out.println(n + ": math -> " + usingmath(n) + ", string length -> " + usingstringlength(n)); } } }

s: Count how many times each character appears in a string (character frequency). As a bonus, group characters BY their frequency.
x: count character frequency countcharacterfrequency.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; import java.util.arraylist; import java.util.linkedhashmap; import java.util.list; import java.util.map; /** * problem: count how many times each character appears in a string * (character frequency). as a bonus, group characters by their frequency. * * example for "programming": * frequency: p=1, r=2, o=1, g=2, a=1, m=2, i=1, n=1 * grouped: 1=[p, o, a, i, n], 2=[r, g, m] * * java terms worth learning here: * - hashmap stores key -> value pairs; here character -> its count. * - linkedhashmap is a hashmap that remembers insertion order, so the * output lists characters in the order they first appeared. * - map.entry is one key-value pair inside a map; entryset() lets you * loop over all of them. */ public class countcharacterfrequency { /** * approach 1: nested loops — no map at all. * * idea: for each position, first check whether the character already * appeared earlier (inner loop over the positions before it). if it * did, skip — it was already reported. otherwise count its * occurrences by scanning forward. pure loops, no collections. */ public static void usingnestedloops(string text) { for (int i = 0; i < text.length(); i++) { char ch = text.charat(i); boolean seenearlier = false; for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) { if (text.charat(j) == ch) { seenearlier = true; break; } } if (seenearlier) { continue; // this character was already counted and printed } int count = 0; for (int j = i; j < text.length(); j++) { if (text.charat(j) == ch) { count++; } } system.out.println(ch + " -> " + count); } } /** * approach 2: the visited[] array technique — still no map. * * idea: same nested counting, but instead of re-scanning backwards * to check "seen earlier", we mark every matched position in a * parallel boolean array so the outer loop skips it later. this is * the classic "visited" pattern you will also see in * easyarrays.countarrayelement. */ public static void usingvisitedarray(string text) { char[] chars = text.tochararray(); boolean[] visited = new boolean[chars.length]; for (int i = 0; i < chars.length; i++) { if (visited[i]) { continue; // already counted inside an earlier group } int count = 1; for (int j = i + 1; j < chars.length; j++) { if (chars[i] == chars[j]) { count++; visited[j] = true; // don't recount this position later } } system.out.println(chars[i] + " -> " + count); } } /** * approach 3: hashmap with the classic containskey check. * * idea: for each character ask "have i counted you before?" if yes, * bump the stored count; if no, start it at 1. this is the verbose * version every java developer should be able to write from memory. */ public static map<character, integer> usingcontainskey(string text) { map<character, integer> frequency = new linkedhashmap<>(); for (char ch : text.tochararray()) { if (frequency.containskey(ch)) { frequency.put(ch, frequency.get(ch) + 1); // seen before -> add 1 } else { frequency.put(ch, 1); // first sighting -> start at 1 } } return frequency; } /** * approach 4: same idea, modern one-liner with merge() (java 8+). * * idea: map.merge(key, 1, integer::sum) means "store 1 if the key is * absent, otherwise add 1 to whatever is already there". one line * replaces the whole if/else — worth recognizing when you read other * people's code. */ public static map<character, integer> usingmerge(string text) { map<character, integer> frequency = new linkedhashmap<>(); for (char ch : text.tochararray()) { frequency.merge(ch, 1, integer::sum); } return frequency; } /** * bonus: flip the frequency map around — group characters by how many * times they appear. * * idea: build a new map of count -> list of characters with that * count. computeifabsent(count, k -> new arraylist<>()) creates the * list the first time a count appears, then we just add to it. */ public static map<integer, list<character>> groupbyfrequency(map<character, integer> frequency) { map<integer, list<character>> grouped = new linkedhashmap<>(); for (map.entry<character, integer> entry : frequency.entryset()) { char ch = entry.getkey(); int count = entry.getvalue(); grouped.computeifabsent(count, k -> new arraylist<>()).add(ch); } return grouped; } public static void main(string[] args) { string input = "programming"; system.out.println("nested loops (no map):"); usingnestedloops(input); system.out.println("visited array (no map):"); usingvisitedarray(input); system.out.println("containskey: " + usingcontainskey(input)); system.out.println("merge: " + usingmerge(input)); system.out.println("grouped: " + groupbyfrequency(usingmerge(input))); } }

x: count vowels per word countvowelsperword.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; import java.util.linkedhashmap; import java.util.map; /** * problem: for each word in a sentence, count how many vowels it has. * * example: * input: "i love java programming" * output: i = 1 * love = 2 * java = 2 * programming = 3 */ public class countvowelsperword { /** * approach 1: a loop inside a loop. * * idea: the outer loop walks the words. for each word we reset count to * 0, then the inner loop walks that word's characters and adds 1 every * time it sees a vowel. resetting count inside the outer loop is the * important bit — that is what makes the count "per word" instead of a * running total for the whole sentence. * * note tolowercase: without it the capital 'i' in "i love" would not * match 'i' and the first word would print 0. */ public static void usingnestedloops(string sentence) { string[] words = sentence.split(" "); for (string word : words) { int count = 0; for (int i = 0; i < word.length(); i++) { char ch = character.tolowercase(word.charat(i)); if (ch == 'a' || ch == 'e' || ch == 'i' || ch == 'o' || ch == 'u') { count++; } } system.out.println(word + " = " + count); } } /** * approach 2: same loops, shorter vowel check. * * idea: instead of five == comparisons, keep the vowels in one string and * ask if it contains the character. "aeiou".indexof(ch) gives the position * of ch, or -1 when it is not there. positions start at 0, so ">= 0" means * it was found, which means it is a vowel. */ public static void usingvowelstring(string sentence) { string vowels = "aeiou"; string[] words = sentence.split(" "); for (string word : words) { int count = 0; for (int i = 0; i < word.length(); i++) { char ch = character.tolowercase(word.charat(i)); if (vowels.indexof(ch) >= 0) { count++; } } system.out.println(word + " = " + count); } } /** * approach 3: store the answers in a map instead of printing them. * * idea: same two loops, but instead of printing straight away we save * word -> count with put(). now the caller can use the counts for * something else, which is usually what an interviewer wants next. * * linkedhashmap keeps the words in sentence order. a plain hashmap would * jumble them and the output would not read like the sentence any more. */ public static map<string, integer> usingmap(string sentence) { map<string, integer> result = new linkedhashmap<>(); string vowels = "aeiou"; for (string word : sentence.split(" ")) { int count = 0; for (int i = 0; i < word.length(); i++) { char ch = character.tolowercase(word.charat(i)); if (vowels.indexof(ch) >= 0) { count++; } } result.put(word, count); } return result; } public static void main(string[] args) { string sentence = "i love java programming"; system.out.println("nested loops:"); usingnestedloops(sentence); system.out.println(); system.out.println("vowel string:"); usingvowelstring(sentence); system.out.println(); system.out.println("map:"); map<string, integer> counts = usingmap(sentence); // walking a map: each entry has a getkey() and a getvalue(). for (map.entry<string, integer> entry : counts.entryset()) { system.out.println(entry.getkey() + " = " + entry.getvalue()); } } }

s: Count how many times a word or substring appears in a string.
x: count word occurrences countwordoccurrences.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; /** * problem: count how many times a word or substring appears in a string. * * examples: * "java is fun and java is powerful", word "java" -> 2 * "banana", substring "ana" -> 1 (non-overlapping) * * the two approaches answer slightly different questions: whole-word * matches vs raw substring matches. pick based on which one is asked. */ public class countwordoccurrences { /** * approach 1: split into words and count exact matches. * * idea: split the sentence on whitespace ("\\s+" means "one or more * whitespace characters"), then count the words that equal() the * target exactly. this is a word match — searching for "java" will * not match "javascript". */ public static int usingsplit(string sentence, string word) { int count = 0; for (string current : sentence.split("\\s+")) { if (current.equals(word)) { count++; } } return count; } /** * approach 2: hop match to match with indexof. * * idea: indexof(target, fromindex) finds the next occurrence at or * after a position, or -1 when there are no more. each time it * hits, we count and jump the search position past this match. this * is a substring match — it sees "ana" inside "banana" regardless * of word boundaries. */ public static int usingindexof(string text, string target) { int count = 0; int fromindex = 0; while ((fromindex = text.indexof(target, fromindex)) != -1) { count++; fromindex += target.length(); // jump past this match (non-overlapping) } return count; } public static void main(string[] args) { string sentence = "java is fun and java is powerful"; system.out.println("word \"java\" (split): " + usingsplit(sentence, "java")); system.out.println("substring \"is\" (indexof): " + usingindexof(sentence, "is")); system.out.println("substring \"ana\" in banana: " + usingindexof("banana", "ana")); } }

x: duplicate characters duplicatecharacters.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; import java.util.linkedhashmap; import java.util.linkedhashset; import java.util.map; import java.util.set; /** * problem: find the characters that appear more than once in a string, * and show how many times each appears. * * example: * input: "programming" * output: r=2, g=2, m=2 * * this is the single-string cousin of * easyarrays.findduplicatestrings, which finds repeated values inside a * string array — same ideas, different input shape. */ public class duplicatecharacters { /** * approach 1: frequency map, then keep only counts above 1. * * idea: count every character with the usual frequency map, then * walk the entries and print just the ones whose count is 2 or * more. simple because the map already did the grouping work. */ public static void usingfrequencymap(string text) { map<character, integer> frequency = new linkedhashmap<>(); for (char ch : text.tochararray()) { frequency.merge(ch, 1, integer::sum); } for (map.entry<character, integer> entry : frequency.entryset()) { if (entry.getvalue() > 1) { system.out.println(entry.getkey() + "=" + entry.getvalue()); } } } /** * approach 2: the set "add returns false" trick. * * idea: lighter-weight when you only need which characters repeat, * not their counts. set.add() returns false when the value was * already there — that false means "this character is a duplicate". */ public static void usingtwosets(string text) { set<character> seen = new linkedhashset<>(); set<character> duplicates = new linkedhashset<>(); for (char ch : text.tochararray()) { if (!seen.add(ch)) { duplicates.add(ch); // add() said "already present" -> a repeat } } for (char ch : duplicates) { system.out.println(ch); } } public static void main(string[] args) { string input = "programming"; system.out.println("frequency map (with counts):"); usingfrequencymap(input); system.out.println("two sets (which chars repeat):"); usingtwosets(input); } }

s: Compute n! (n FACTORIAL) — the product of all numbers from 1 to n.
x: factorial factorial.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; /** * problem: compute n! (n factorial) — the product of all numbers from * 1 to n. * * example: * input: 5 * output: 120 (5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1) * * note: factorials grow insanely fast. int overflows at 13!, and even * long overflows at 21! — that is why these methods return long, and * why anything bigger needs java.math.biginteger. */ public class factorial { /** * approach 1: loop and multiply. * * idea: start the result at 1 (not 0 — multiplying by 0 would wipe * everything out) and multiply by each number from 2 up to n. */ public static long usingloop(int n) { long result = 1; for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) { result = result * i; } return result; } /** * approach 2: recursion (a method that calls itself). * * idea: n! is n x (n-1)! by definition, so the method restates the * definition. "n <= 1" is the base case that stops the chain — * without it the method would call itself forever. */ public static long usingrecursion(int n) { if (n <= 1) { return 1; // base case: 0! = 1 and 1! = 1 } return n * usingrecursion(n - 1); // recursive case } public static void main(string[] args) { system.out.println("5! loop=" + usingloop(5) + ", recursion=" + usingrecursion(5)); system.out.println("20! loop=" + usingloop(20) + ", recursion=" + usingrecursion(20)); } }

s: Print the Fibonacci series — the sequence where every number is the sum of the two before it: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ...
x: fibonacci series fibonacciseries.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; /** * problem: print the fibonacci series — the sequence where every number * is the sum of the two before it: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ... * * example: * input: 7 (how many numbers to print) * output: 0 1 1 2 3 5 8 */ public class fibonacciseries { /** * approach 1: iterate, carrying the last two numbers. * * idea: you only ever need the previous two numbers to compute the * next one, so carry them in two variables (a and b) and slide them * forward each step: the new "a" is the old "b", the new "b" is their * sum. think of it as a two-window frame sliding along the series. */ public static void printiterative(int howmany) { int a = 0; // first number of the series int b = 1; // second number of the series for (int i = 0; i < howmany; i++) { system.out.print(a + " "); int next = a + b; // the next fibonacci number a = b; // slide the window one step forward b = next; } system.out.println(); } /** * approach 2: recursion (a method that calls itself). * * idea: fib(n) is fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) by definition, so the method * literally restates the definition. the if for n <= 1 is the base * case — the condition that stops the method from calling itself * forever. * * beautiful, but wasteful: fib(10) recomputes fib(8), which * recomputes fib(7)... the same values are calculated over and over. * fine for small n; approach 1 is what you would actually use. */ public static int fib(int n) { if (n <= 1) { return n; // base case: fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1 } return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); // recursive case: restate the definition } public static void main(string[] args) { int howmany = 7; system.out.println("iterative:"); printiterative(howmany); system.out.println("recursive:"); for (int i = 0; i < howmany; i++) { system.out.print(fib(i) + " "); } system.out.println(); } }

s: Find the FIRST and the LAST character in a string that appear exactly once (non-repeated characters).
x: first and last non repeated char firstandlastnonrepeatedchar.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; import java.util.linkedhashmap; import java.util.map; /** * problem: find the first and the last character in a string that appear * exactly once (non-repeated characters). * * example for "programming": * frequencies: p=1, r=2, o=1, g=2, a=1, m=2, i=1, n=1 * non-repeated characters in order: p, o, a, i, n * output: first = p, last = n */ public class firstandlastnonrepeatedchar { /** * approach 1: nested loops with a visited array. * * idea: for each character, scan the rest of the string counting its * duplicates and marking those positions "visited" so they are not * recounted. a character whose final count is 1 is non-repeated: the * first one we meet is the answer for "first", and every later one * keeps overwriting "last". */ public static void usingnestedloops(string text) { char[] chars = text.tochararray(); boolean[] visited = new boolean[chars.length]; character firstnonrepeated = null; // character (object) so it can hold null = "not found yet" character lastnonrepeated = null; for (int i = 0; i < chars.length; i++) { if (visited[i]) { continue; // already counted inside an earlier group } int count = 1; for (int j = i + 1; j < chars.length; j++) { if (chars[i] == chars[j]) { count++; visited[j] = true; } } if (count == 1) { if (firstnonrepeated == null) { firstnonrepeated = chars[i]; // only the very first one lands here } lastnonrepeated = chars[i]; // every non-repeated char updates this } } system.out.println("first non-repeated: " + firstnonrepeated); system.out.println("last non-repeated: " + lastnonrepeated); } /** * approach 2: count everything first, then read the counts in order. * * idea: split the job into two simple passes. pass 1 builds the full * frequency map with a linkedhashmap — insertion order matters because * it lets us find the first non-repeated character just by reading the * map in order. pass 2 walks the map: the first entry with count 1 is * "first", and we keep updating "last" with every count-1 entry. */ public static void usingfrequencymap(string text) { map<character, integer> frequency = new linkedhashmap<>(); for (char ch : text.tochararray()) { frequency.merge(ch, 1, integer::sum); } character firstnonrepeated = null; character lastnonrepeated = null; for (map.entry<character, integer> entry : frequency.entryset()) { if (entry.getvalue() == 1) { if (firstnonrepeated == null) { firstnonrepeated = entry.getkey(); } lastnonrepeated = entry.getkey(); } } system.out.println("first non-repeated: " + firstnonrepeated); system.out.println("last non-repeated: " + lastnonrepeated); } public static void main(string[] args) { string input = "programming"; system.out.println("nested loops:"); usingnestedloops(input); system.out.println("frequency map:"); usingfrequencymap(input); } }

s: Find the longest AND the shortest word in a sentence.
x: longest and shortest word longestandshortestword.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; import java.util.arrays; import java.util.comparator; /** * problem: find the longest and the shortest word in a sentence. * * example: * input: "i am the tribal chief" * output: longest = "tribal", shortest = "i" * * note: on ties these approaches return the first word with that length. */ public class longestandshortestword { /** * approach 1: split and track both champions in one pass. * * idea: carry two champions through the word list — the longest and * the shortest seen so far. both start as the first word (starting * shortest at "" would never lose, since no word is shorter than * empty). strict ">" / "<" comparisons mean ties keep the earlier * word. */ public static void usingloop(string sentence) { string[] words = sentence.split(" "); string longest = words[0]; string shortest = words[0]; for (string word : words) { if (word.length() > longest.length()) { longest = word; } if (word.length() < shortest.length()) { shortest = word; } } system.out.println("longest=" + longest + ", shortest=" + shortest); } /** * approach 2: java 8 streams. * * idea: stream the words twice — once asking for the max() by * length, once for the min(). comparator.comparingint(string::length) * means "compare words by their length", and the optional results * are unwrapped with orelse("") for empty input. */ public static void usingstreams(string sentence) { string[] words = sentence.split(" "); string longest = arrays.stream(words) .max(comparator.comparingint(string::length)) .orelse(""); string shortest = arrays.stream(words) .min(comparator.comparingint(string::length)) .orelse(""); system.out.println("longest=" + longest + ", shortest=" + shortest); } public static void main(string[] args) { string input = "i am the tribal chief"; system.out.println("loop: "); usingloop(input); system.out.println("streams: "); usingstreams(input); } }

s: Find the character that appears MOST OFTEN in a string.
x: most frequent character mostfrequentcharacter.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; import java.util.linkedhashmap; import java.util.map; /** * problem: find the character that appears most often in a string. * * example: * input: "banana" * output: 'a' (appears 3 times) * * note: on a tie this returns the character that reached the top count * first in reading order ("success" -> 's', even though 'c' also * appears twice). */ public class mostfrequentcharacter { /** * approach 1: frequency map, then scan for the champion. * * idea: this problem is two smaller problems chained. step 1 is the * familiar character frequency count (see countcharacterfrequency). * step 2 walks the map keeping track of the entry with the highest * count — ">" means the first character to reach the top count wins * ties. */ public static char usingfrequencymap(string text) { map<character, integer> frequency = new linkedhashmap<>(); for (char ch : text.tochararray()) { frequency.merge(ch, 1, integer::sum); } char mostfrequent = ' '; int highestcount = 0; for (map.entry<character, integer> entry : frequency.entryset()) { if (entry.getvalue() > highestcount) { highestcount = entry.getvalue(); mostfrequent = entry.getkey(); } } return mostfrequent; } /** * approach 2: let the stream pick the max entry. * * idea: same frequency map, but the champion scan is expressed as * max() over the entry set. map.entry.comparingbyvalue() tells the * stream to compare entries by their counts. max() returns an * optional, which we unwrap with orelsethrow(). */ public static char usingstreams(string text) { map<character, integer> frequency = new linkedhashmap<>(); for (char ch : text.tochararray()) { frequency.merge(ch, 1, integer::sum); } return frequency.entryset().stream() .max(map.entry.comparingbyvalue()) .orelsethrow() .getkey(); } public static void main(string[] args) { string[] samples = { "banana", "success" }; for (string sample : samples) { system.out.println(sample + ": map -> " + usingfrequencymap(sample) + ", streams -> " + usingstreams(sample)); } } }

s: Check whether a number is PRIME — a number greater than 1 that is divisible only by 1 and itself.
x: prime number primenumber.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; /** * problem: check whether a number is prime — a number greater than 1 that * is divisible only by 1 and itself. * * examples: 7 -> prime, 12 -> not prime (12 = 3 x 4), 2 -> prime * * edge cases to remember: 0 and 1 are not prime by definition, and 2 is * prime (the only even one). */ public class primenumber { /** * approach 1: try every divisor up to n / 2. * * idea: a divisor of n can never be bigger than n / 2 (the smallest * possible partner is 2, and n / 2 x 2 = n already). so testing * divisors 2 up to n/2 is enough. n % i == 0 means "i divides n * exactly" -> not prime. */ public static boolean isprimeuptohalf(int n) { if (n < 2) { return false; // 0 and 1 are not prime } for (int i = 2; i <= n / 2; i++) { if (n % i == 0) { return false; // found an exact divisor -> not prime } } return true; // nothing divided n -> prime } /** * approach 2: try divisors only up to the square root of n. * * idea: divisors come in pairs. if n = a x b and a is bigger than * sqrt(n), then b must be smaller than sqrt(n) — so any pair would * already have been found by its smaller member. that is why checking * up to i * i <= n is enough; we write "i * i <= n" instead of * "i <= sqrt(n)" to stay with integers and avoid floating point. */ public static boolean isprimeuptosquareroot(int n) { if (n < 2) { return false; } for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; i++) { if (n % i == 0) { return false; } } return true; } public static void main(string[] args) { int[] candidates = { 1, 2, 7, 12, 29 }; for (int n : candidates) { system.out.println(n + ": up to n/2 -> " + isprimeuptohalf(n) + ", up to sqrt -> " + isprimeuptosquareroot(n)); } } }

s: Remove duplicate characters from a string, keeping the first occurrence of each character in its original position.
x: remove duplicates from string removeduplicatesfromstring.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; import java.util.linkedhashset; import java.util.set; /** * problem: remove duplicate characters from a string, keeping the first * occurrence of each character in its original position. * * example: * input: "programming" * output: "progamin" * * java terms worth learning here: * - linkedhashset is a set (so it silently refuses duplicates) that also * remembers insertion order. plain hashset would dedupe too, but the * characters could come out in any order. * - string.tochararray() converts a string into a char[] so you can loop * over it with a for-each loop. */ public class removeduplicatesfromstring { /** * approach 1: feed every character through a linkedhashset. * * idea: add each character to the set — duplicates are ignored * automatically — then read the set back into a string. the set does * all the dedupe work for us. */ public static string usinglinkedhashset(string text) { set<character> unique = new linkedhashset<>(); for (char ch : text.tochararray()) { unique.add(ch); // already present? add() just does nothing } stringbuilder result = new stringbuilder(); for (char ch : unique) { result.append(ch); } return result.tostring(); } /** * approach 2: build the answer, skipping characters already in it. * * idea: grow the result one character at a time; before appending, * check whether the result already contains that character * (stringbuilder.indexof returns -1 when not found). no extra * collection needed — but the repeated indexof scan is exactly the * work the set was doing for us in approach 1. */ public static string usingindexof(string text) { stringbuilder result = new stringbuilder(); for (char ch : text.tochararray()) { if (result.indexof(string.valueof(ch)) == -1) { // -1 = not seen yet result.append(ch); } } return result.tostring(); } public static void main(string[] args) { string input = "programming"; system.out.println("linkedhashset: " + usinglinkedhashset(input)); system.out.println("indexof check: " + usingindexof(input)); } }

s: Reverse the digits of a number.
x: reverse the number reversethenumber.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; /** * problem: reverse the digits of a number. * * example: * input: 1234 * output: 4321 * * java terms worth learning here: * - num % 10 gives the last digit of a number (remainder after dividing * by 10). example: 1234 % 10 = 4. * - num / 10 drops the last digit (integer division throws away the * fraction). example: 1234 / 10 = 123. * together they let you peel a number apart digit by digit. */ public class reversethenumber { /** * approach 1: peel digits with math (the classic answer). * * idea: repeatedly take the last digit (num % 10) and append it to the * result by shifting the result one decimal place left (rev * 10) and * adding the digit. then chop the used digit off num (num / 10). * * walkthrough for 1234: * digit 4 -> rev = 0*10 + 4 = 4 * digit 3 -> rev = 4*10 + 3 = 43 * digit 2 -> rev = 43*10 + 2 = 432 * digit 1 -> rev = 432*10 + 1 = 4321 */ public static int usingmath(int num) { int reversed = 0; while (num != 0) { int lastdigit = num % 10; // peel off the last digit reversed = reversed * 10 + lastdigit; // append it to the result num = num / 10; // drop the used digit } return reversed; } /** * approach 2: turn it into a string and reverse that. * * idea: reversing text is a solved problem (stringbuilder.reverse()), * so convert the number to a string, reverse, convert back. fewer * moving parts, at the cost of a type conversion round-trip. */ public static int usingstring(int num) { string reversedtext = new stringbuilder(string.valueof(num)).reverse().tostring(); return integer.parseint(reversedtext); // parse the text back into an int } public static void main(string[] args) { int input = 1234; system.out.println("math: " + usingmath(input)); system.out.println("string: " + usingstring(input)); } }

s: Reverse the order of WORDS in a sentence (the words themselves stay intact).
x: reverse the sentence reversethesentence.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; import java.util.arrays; import java.util.collections; import java.util.list; /** * problem: reverse the order of words in a sentence (the words themselves * stay intact). * * example: * input: "i am the tribal chief" * output: "chief tribal the am i" * * java terms worth learning here: * - string.split(" ") breaks a string into a string[] around each space. * - string.join(" ", pieces) glues parts together with the separator * between them — no trailing space to clean up afterwards. */ public class reversethesentence { /** * approach 1: split, then collect words backwards. * * idea: split the sentence into words, walk the array from the last * word to the first, and append each with a space. we add the space * before every word except the first one, so there is no stray space * at the end. */ public static string usingloop(string sentence) { string[] words = sentence.split(" "); stringbuilder reversed = new stringbuilder(); for (int i = words.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) { if (reversed.length() > 0) { reversed.append(" "); // separator goes between words, not after } reversed.append(words[i]); } return reversed.tostring(); } /** * approach 2: split, reverse the list, join (the everyday answer). * * idea: turn the array into a list so we can use collections.reverse() * on it, then glue everything back with string.join(). same result, * almost no manual index work. */ public static string usingcollections(string sentence) { list<string> words = arrays.aslist(sentence.split(" ")); collections.reverse(words); // reverses the list in place return string.join(" ", words); } public static void main(string[] args) { string input = "i am the tribal chief"; system.out.println("loop: " + usingloop(input)); system.out.println("collections: " + usingcollections(input)); } }

s: Reverse a string.
x: reverse the string reversethestring.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; /** * problem: reverse a string. * * example: * input: "madan" * output: "nadam" * * java terms worth learning here: * - string is immutable: once created, a string object can never change. * that is why "rev = rev + ch" inside a loop silently creates a brand * new string object on every iteration — wasteful. * - stringbuilder is the mutable companion of string, designed exactly * for building text piece by piece. prefer it inside loops. */ public class reversethestring { /** * approach 1: walk backwards with a stringbuilder. * * idea: read the characters from the last index down to the first and * append each one. appending to a stringbuilder just grows the same * object, so no throwaway strings are created. */ public static string usingloop(string text) { stringbuilder reversed = new stringbuilder(); for (int i = text.length() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { reversed.append(text.charat(i)); // charat(i) = the character at index i } return reversed.tostring(); // convert back to a regular string } /** * approach 2: let stringbuilder do it (the everyday answer). * * idea: stringbuilder already ships with a reverse() method. knowing * your standard library is a skill in itself — in real test automation * code you would write this one-liner, not a loop. */ public static string usingstringbuilderreverse(string text) { return new stringbuilder(text).reverse().tostring(); } public static void main(string[] args) { string input = "madan"; system.out.println("loop: " + usingloop(input)); system.out.println("stringbuilder: " + usingstringbuilderreverse(input)); } }

s: Separate a mixed string into three groups — letters, digits, and special characters — keeping each group's original order.
x: separate character types separatecharactertypes.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; /** * problem: separate a mixed string into three groups — letters, digits, * and special characters — keeping each group's original order. * * example: * input: "abcd1234!#$" * output: alphabets: abcd | numbers: 1234 | specials: !#$ */ public class separatecharactertypes { /** * approach 1: sort each character with the character class. * * idea: walk the string once; character.isletter() and * character.isdigit() route each character into one of three * stringbuilders. anything that is neither letter nor digit lands in * "specials" by elimination. */ public static void usingcharacterclass(string text) { stringbuilder alphabets = new stringbuilder(); stringbuilder numbers = new stringbuilder(); stringbuilder specials = new stringbuilder(); for (char ch : text.tochararray()) { if (character.isletter(ch)) { alphabets.append(ch); } else if (character.isdigit(ch)) { numbers.append(ch); } else { specials.append(ch); // neither letter nor digit -> special } } system.out.println("alphabets: " + alphabets); system.out.println("numbers: " + numbers); system.out.println("specials: " + specials); } /** * approach 2: regex subtraction with replaceall. * * idea: build each group by deleting everything that does not belong * to it. "[^a-za-z]" is a regex negated character class — it matches * any single character that is not a letter — so replacing it with "" * leaves only letters behind. same trick with 0-9 for digits, and * the inverse class for specials. */ public static void usingregex(string text) { string alphabets = text.replaceall("[^a-za-z]", ""); string numbers = text.replaceall("[^0-9]", ""); string specials = text.replaceall("[a-za-z0-9]", ""); // delete letters and digits system.out.println("alphabets: " + alphabets); system.out.println("numbers: " + numbers); system.out.println("specials: " + specials); } public static void main(string[] args) { string input = "abcd1234!#$"; system.out.println("character class:"); usingcharacterclass(input); system.out.println("regex:"); usingregex(input); } }

s: Add up the digits of a number.
x: sum of digits sumofdigits.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; /** * problem: add up the digits of a number. * * example: * input: 1234 * output: 10 (1 + 2 + 3 + 4) */ public class sumofdigits { /** * approach 1: peel digits with math. * * idea: the same % 10 and / 10 pair used in reversethenumber — * % 10 hands you the last digit, / 10 removes it. add each peeled * digit to a running total. */ public static int usingmath(int num) { int sum = 0; while (num != 0) { sum = sum + (num % 10); // add the last digit num = num / 10; // then drop it } return sum; } /** * approach 2: walk the digits as characters. * * idea: turn the number into a string and add up each character. * "ch - '0'" converts a digit character to its int value: characters * '0'..'9' sit next to each other in the character table, so * '7' - '0' is simply 7. (character.getnumericvalue(ch) does the * same job with a longer name.) */ public static int usingstring(int num) { int sum = 0; for (char ch : string.valueof(num).tochararray()) { sum = sum + (ch - '0'); } return sum; } public static void main(string[] args) { int input = 1234; system.out.println("math: " + usingmath(input)); system.out.println("string: " + usingstring(input)); } }

s: Swap the case of every letter in a string — uppercase becomes lowercase and lowercase becomes uppercase. Non-letters stay as they are.
x: swap character case swapcharactercase.java package com.sdet.studyplan.easystrings; /** * problem: swap the case of every letter in a string — uppercase becomes * lowercase and lowercase becomes uppercase. non-letters stay as they are. * * example: * input: "hexaware123" * output: "hexaware123" * * java terms worth learning here: * - the character class is the wrapper class for the primitive char. * it carries helpful static methods like isuppercase(), islowercase(), * touppercase() and tolowercase(), so you rarely manipulate raw * character codes yourself. */ public class swapcharactercase { /** * approach 1: check each character with the character class. * * idea: walk through the string one char at a time. if it is an * uppercase letter, append its lowercase form; if lowercase, append * its uppercase form; otherwise (digits, spaces, punctuation) append * it unchanged. that final "otherwise" branch is easy to forget — * without it, digits would silently disappear from the output. */ public static string usingcharacterclass(string text) { stringbuilder result = new stringbuilder(); for (int i = 0; i < text.length(); i++) { char ch = text.charat(i); if (character.isuppercase(ch)) { result.append(character.tolowercase(ch)); } else if (character.islowercase(ch)) { result.append(character.touppercase(ch)); } else { result.append(ch); // not a letter -> keep it as it is } } return result.tostring(); } /** * approach 2: same logic, ternary operator style. * * idea: identical checks, but each character is converted in a single * expression using the ternary operator (condition ? valueiftrue : * valueiffalse). handy when each branch is one short expression. */ public static string usingternary(string text) { stringbuilder result = new stringbuilder(); for (int i = 0; i < text.length(); i++) { char ch = text.charat(i); char swapped = character.isuppercase(ch) ? character.tolowercase(ch) : character.touppercase(ch); // note: touppercase/tolowercase return the char unchanged when // it is not a letter, so no extra else-branch is needed here. result.append(swapped); } return result.tostring(); } public static void main(string[] args) { string input = "hexaware123"; system.out.println("character class: " + usingcharacterclass(input)); system.out.println("ternary: " + usingternary(input)); } }

s: Reading a sheet into a data table for a DataProvider. Tap a program to open its code. Every one of these is your own, written with plain loops.

import java.io.fileinputstream; import java.io.ioexception; import java.util.arraylist; import java.util.linkedhashmap; import java.util.list; import java.util.map; import org.apache.poi.ss.usermodel.dataformatter; import org.apache.poi.ss.usermodel.row; import org.apache.poi.xssf.usermodel.xssfsheet; import org.apache.poi.xssf.usermodel.xssfworkbook; /** * turn an excel sheet into a data table: a list of maps, one map per * data row, keyed by the header names. * * for apache.xlsx: * row 0 (header): username | password * row 1: balaji | sannasi#5835 * row 2: yugan | 123557 * * becomes: * [ {username=balaji, password=sannasi#5835}, * {username=yugan, password=123557} ] * * this is the standard shape for data-driven testing: hand the list to * a testng @dataprovider and each map becomes one test run — one login * attempt per row, with the code never hardcoding the values. */ public class datatable { /** * reads the first sheet of the given .xlsx file and returns one map * per data row, where each key is the header of that column. */ public static list<map<string, string>> readastable(string filename) throws ioexception { list<map<string, string>> table = new arraylist<>(); try (fileinputstream file = new fileinputstream(filename); xssfworkbook workbook = new xssfworkbook(file)) { xssfsheet sheet = workbook.getsheetat(0); // dataformatter gives the text as excel displays it — without // it, a numeric cell like 123557 reads back as "123557.0". dataformatter formatter = new dataformatter(); // step 1: read the header row — it provides the map keys. row headerrow = sheet.getrow(0); list<string> headers = new arraylist<>(); for (int j = 0; j < headerrow.getphysicalnumberofcells(); j++) { headers.add(formatter.formatcellvalue(headerrow.getcell(j))); } // step 2: for each data row, pair every cell with its header. // getlastrownum() is the index of the final row. looping to // getphysicalnumberofrows() instead silently drops trailing rows // whenever the sheet has a blank line in the middle, because the // physical count is smaller than the last index. for (int i = 1; i <= sheet.getlastrownum(); i++) { row row = sheet.getrow(i); if (row == null) { continue; } map<string, string> rowdata = new linkedhashmap<>(); for (int j = 0; j < headers.size(); j++) { string cellvalue = row.getcell(j) == null ? "" : formatter.formatcellvalue(row.getcell(j)); rowdata.put(headers.get(j), cellvalue); } table.add(rowdata); } } return table; } public static void main(string[] args) throws ioexception { list<map<string, string>> table = readastable("apache.xlsx"); // reading the data back by column name — no magic column indexes. for (map<string, string> row : table) { system.out.println("username=" + row.get("username") + ", password=" + row.get("password")); } } } read excel read and print every row of an .xlsx file with apache poi. the poi vocabulary maps 1:1 to what you see in excel: workbook -> the whole file (xssfworkbook = .xlsx forma... readexcel.java package com.sdet.studyplan.excel; import java.io.fileinputstream; import java.io.ioexception; import java.nio.file.files; import java.nio.file.path; import org.apache.poi.ss.usermodel.cell; import org.apache.poi.ss.usermodel.dataformatter; import org.apache.poi.ss.usermodel.row; import org.apache.poi.xssf.usermodel.xssfsheet; import org.apache.poi.xssf.usermodel.xssfworkbook; /** * read and print every row of an .xlsx file with apache poi. * * the poi vocabulary maps 1:1 to what you see in excel: * workbook -> the whole file (xssfworkbook = .xlsx format) * sheet -> one tab at the bottom (xssfsheet) * row -> one horizontal line (row) * cell -> one box in the grid (cell) * * why keep test data in excel at all? so data can change (new logins, * new environments) without touching the test code. * * try-with-resources note: "try (xssfworkbook workbook = ...)" closes * the workbook and the file automatically when the block ends — no * manual close() needed, even if an exception is thrown. */ public class readexcel { public static void main(string[] args) throws ioexception { path excelpath = path.of("apache.xlsx"); if (files.notexists(excelpath)) { throw new ioexception("excel file not found: " + excelpath.toabsolutepath()); } try (fileinputstream file = new fileinputstream(excelpath.tofile()); xssfworkbook workbook = new xssfworkbook(file)) { xssfsheet sheet = workbook.getsheetat(0); // first tab // dataformatter renders a cell the way excel displays it. // we need it because numeric cells come back as doubles: // cell.tostring() on the password 123557 would print // "123557.0" — a wrong password in a real login test! dataformatter formatter = new dataformatter(); // getphysicalnumberofrows counts only rows that actually have // content — safer than getlastrownum() for typical files. int rowcount = sheet.getphysicalnumberofrows(); // start at row 1: row 0 is the header (username | password). for (int i = 1; i < rowcount; i++) { row row = sheet.getrow(i); if (row == null) { continue; // blank line inside the sheet } for (int j = 0; j < row.getphysicalnumberofcells(); j++) { cell cell = row.getcell(j); if (cell != null) { system.out.print(formatter.formatcellvalue(cell) + " "); } } system.out.println(); } } } }

x: read excel readexcel.java package com.sdet.studyplan.excel; import java.io.fileinputstream; import java.io.ioexception; import java.nio.file.files; import java.nio.file.path; import org.apache.poi.ss.usermodel.cell; import org.apache.poi.ss.usermodel.dataformatter; import org.apache.poi.ss.usermodel.row; import org.apache.poi.xssf.usermodel.xssfsheet; import org.apache.poi.xssf.usermodel.xssfworkbook; /** * read and print every row of an .xlsx file with apache poi. * * the poi vocabulary maps 1:1 to what you see in excel: * workbook -> the whole file (xssfworkbook = .xlsx format) * sheet -> one tab at the bottom (xssfsheet) * row -> one horizontal line (row) * cell -> one box in the grid (cell) * * why keep test data in excel at all? so data can change (new logins, * new environments) without touching the test code. * * try-with-resources note: "try (xssfworkbook workbook = ...)" closes * the workbook and the file automatically when the block ends — no * manual close() needed, even if an exception is thrown. */ public class readexcel { public static void main(string[] args) throws ioexception { path excelpath = path.of("apache.xlsx"); if (files.notexists(excelpath)) { throw new ioexception("excel file not found: " + excelpath.toabsolutepath()); } try (fileinputstream file = new fileinputstream(excelpath.tofile()); xssfworkbook workbook = new xssfworkbook(file)) { xssfsheet sheet = workbook.getsheetat(0); // first tab // dataformatter renders a cell the way excel displays it. // we need it because numeric cells come back as doubles: // cell.tostring() on the password 123557 would print // "123557.0" — a wrong password in a real login test! dataformatter formatter = new dataformatter(); // getphysicalnumberofrows counts only rows that actually have // content — safer than getlastrownum() for typical files. int rowcount = sheet.getphysicalnumberofrows(); // start at row 1: row 0 is the header (username | password). for (int i = 1; i < rowcount; i++) { row row = sheet.getrow(i); if (row == null) { continue; // blank line inside the sheet } for (int j = 0; j < row.getphysicalnumberofcells(); j++) { cell cell = row.getcell(j); if (cell != null) { system.out.print(formatter.formatcellvalue(cell) + " "); } } system.out.println(); } } } }

import java.util.arrays; import java.util.list; import java.util.function.predicate; import java.util.stream.collectors; /** * java 8 core vocabulary, in one file: functional interface, lambda, and * predicate. * * - functional interface: an interface with exactly one abstract method. * because there is only one method to implement, java lets you supply * that single method inline instead of writing a whole class. * predicate<t> is the classic example: its one method is * "boolean test(t value)". * * - lambda: the inline implementation of that single method. * read "number -> number % 2 == 0" as: "take a number, return whether * it is even". left of the arrow are the parameters, right is the body. * * why a test engineer cares: selenium's waits, stream filters, and most * modern java test libraries accept lambdas, so you will read and write * them constantly. */ public class lambdaandpredicate { public static void main(string[] args) { // a predicate<integer> named iseven: one input, true/false answer. predicate<integer> iseven = number -> number % 2 == 0; // call its single method, test(), directly. system.out.println("iseven.test(4): " + iseven.test(4)); system.out.println("iseven.test(7): " + iseven.test(7)); // the same logic before java 8 took an anonymous class — this is // what the lambda replaces (no need to write this way anymore): predicate<integer> isevenoldstyle = new predicate<integer>() { @override public boolean test(integer number) { return number % 2 == 0; } }; system.out.println("old style: " + isevenoldstyle.test(4)); // where lambdas really shine: passing behavior into a method. // stream.filter() keeps only the elements for which the predicate // returns true. list<integer> numbers = arrays.aslist(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8); list<integer> evens = numbers.stream() .filter(iseven) // reuse the same predicate object .collect(collectors.tolist()); system.out.println("filtered evens: " + evens); // predicates combine: and(), or(), negate(). predicate<integer> ispositive = number -> number > 0; list<integer> mixed = arrays.aslist(-4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4); list<integer> positiveevens = mixed.stream() .filter(iseven.and(ispositive)) // both must be true .collect(collectors.tolist()); system.out.println("positive evens: " + positiveevens); } }

.equals() checks whether the text is the same. */ public class palindrome { /** * approach 1: two pointers walking towards each other. * * idea: place one finger on the first character and one on the last. * compare them; if they differ, it cannot be a palindrome. otherwise * move both fingers one step inwards and repeat until they meet. */ public static boolean usingtwopointers(string text) { int left = 0; int right = text.length() - 1;
