x: most frequent prefix mostfrequentprefix.java package com.sdet.studyplan.medium; import java.util.linkedhashmap; import java.util.map; /** * problem: given an array of words, find the prefix shared by the most * words. when several prefixes tie, the longest one wins — "sql" beats * "s" because it describes the shared start more precisely. * * example: * input: ["sqlex", "sqlengine", "sqlite", "sql", "java"] * output: "sql" (4 words start with it) * * don't confuse this with the longest common prefix problem (see * longestcommonprefix), which asks for the longest prefix shared by all * words — a different question. */ public class mostfrequentprefix { /** * approach: count every prefix of every word, then pick the best. * * idea: a word contributes +1 to each of its prefixes ("sqlex" votes * for "s", "sq", "sql", "sqle", "sqlex"). after counting all votes * in a map, a prefix's count is exactly the number of words that * start with it. then we scan the map: strictly-greater count takes * the lead, and an equal count only takes the lead when the new * prefix is longer (the tie-break rule above). */ public static string usingprefixvotes(string[] words) { map<string, integer> prefixvotes = new linkedhashmap<>(); // every word votes for all of its prefixes. for (string word : words) { for (int end = 1; end <= word.length(); end++) { string prefix = word.substring(0, end); // substring(0, end) = prefix of length "end" prefixvotes.merge(prefix, 1, integer::sum); } } string bestprefix = ""; int bestcount = 0; for (map.entry<string, integer> entry : prefixvotes.entryset()) { string prefix = entry.getkey(); int count = entry.getvalue(); if (count > bestcount || (count == bestcount && prefix.length() > bestprefix.length())) { bestprefix = prefix; bestcount = count; } } return bestprefix; } public static void main(string[] args) { string[] words = { "sqlex", "sqlengine", "sqlite", "sql", "java" }; system.out.println("most frequent prefix: " + usingprefixvotes(words)); } }

s: Check whether a string is a PALINDROME — it reads the same forwards and backwards.
x: palindrome palindrome.java package com.sdet.studyplan.medium; /** * problem: check whether a string is a palindrome — it reads the same * forwards and backwards. * * examples: "madam" -> true, "racecar" -> true, "hello" -> false * * java gotcha worth learning: compare strings with .equals(), never with * ==. the == operator checks whether two references point to the same * object in memory; .equals() checks whether the text is the same. */ public class palindrome { /** * approach 1: two pointers walking towards each other. * * idea: place one finger on the first character and one on the last. * compare them; if they differ, it cannot be a palindrome. otherwise * move both fingers one step inwards and repeat until they meet. */ public static boolean usingtwopointers(string text) { int left = 0; int right = text.length() - 1; while (left < right) { if (text.charat(left) != text.charat(right)) { return false; // mismatch found -> not a palindrome } left++; right--; } return true; // every pair matched } /** * approach 2: reverse it and compare with the original. * * idea: a palindrome equals its own reversal, so reverse the string * and check equality. shorter to write, at the cost of building a * second string. */ public static boolean usingreverse(string text) { string reversed = new stringbuilder(text).reverse().tostring(); return text.equals(reversed); // .equals(), not == } public static void main(string[] args) { string[] samples = { "madam", "racecar", "hello" }; for (string sample : samples) { system.out.println(sample + ": two pointers -> " + usingtwopointers(sample) + ", reverse -> " + usingreverse(sample)); } } }

s: Remove duplicate values from an array.
x: remove duplicates removeduplicates.java package com.sdet.studyplan.medium; import java.util.hashset; import java.util.linkedhashset; import java.util.set; /** * problem: remove duplicate values from an array. * * example: * input: [2, 4, 4, 5, 5, 3, 4, 5] * output: [2, 4, 5, 3] (order depends on the set you choose — see below) * * this file is about one lesson: which set you pick changes the output. * - hashset -> dedupes, but makes no promise about order * - linkedhashset -> dedupes and keeps first-seen order * for the sorted-array two-pointer version, see * easyarrays.removeduplicatesfromarray; for the java 8 one-liner, see * removeduplicatesstream in this package. */ public class removeduplicates { /** * approach 1: hashset. * * idea: throw everything into a hashset; duplicates are ignored. * fine when you only care about which values exist, not their order. */ public static set<integer> usinghashset(int[] nums) { set<integer> unique = new hashset<>(); for (int num : nums) { unique.add(num); } return unique; } /** * approach 2: linkedhashset. * * idea: same dedupe behavior, but the set remembers the order in * which values first appeared, so the output reads naturally. when * someone says "remove duplicates" without mentioning order, this is * usually the behavior they picture. */ public static set<integer> usinglinkedhashset(int[] nums) { set<integer> unique = new linkedhashset<>(); for (int num : nums) { unique.add(num); } return unique; } public static void main(string[] args) { int[] input = { 2, 4, 4, 5, 5, 3, 4, 5 }; system.out.println("hashset (no order guarantee): " + usinghashset(input)); system.out.println("linkedhashset (first-seen): " + usinglinkedhashset(input)); } }

s: Walk through a string; every time the target character 'a' appears, replace it with as many stars as its occurrence number — the 1st 'a' becomes "*", the 2nd becomes "...
x: replace nth occurrence replacenthoccurrence.java package com.sdet.studyplan.medium; /** * problem: walk through a string; every time the target character 'a' * appears, replace it with as many stars as its occurrence number — * the 1st 'a' becomes "*", the 2nd becomes "**", the 3rd becomes "***". * * example: * input: "ananya" * output: "*n**ny***" * (1st 'a' -> *, 2nd 'a' -> **, 3rd 'a' -> ***) */ public class replacenthoccurrence { /** * approach 1: counter with an inner loop for the stars. * * idea: keep a counter of how many 'a' characters we have met so far. * on meeting the next 'a', append "counter" stars (inner loop does * the repeating), then bump the counter. any other character passes * through unchanged. */ public static string usinginnerloop(string text, char target) { stringbuilder result = new stringbuilder(); int occurrence = 0; for (int i = 0; i < text.length(); i++) { char ch = text.charat(i); if (ch == target) { occurrence++; // which 'a' is this? 1st, 2nd, 3rd... for (int star = 0; star < occurrence; star++) { result.append('*'); } } else { result.append(ch); } } return result.tostring(); } /** * approach 2: string.repeat() (java 11) instead of the inner loop. * * idea: identical logic, but "*".repeat(occurrence) produces the run * of stars in one call. string.repeat() is a handy java 11 addition — * good to know it exists before hand-writing repeat loops. */ public static string usingstringrepeat(string text, char target) { stringbuilder result = new stringbuilder(); int occurrence = 0; for (int i = 0; i < text.length(); i++) { char ch = text.charat(i); if (ch == target) { occurrence++; result.append("*".repeat(occurrence)); } else { result.append(ch); } } return result.tostring(); } public static void main(string[] args) { string input = "ananya"; system.out.println("inner loop: " + usinginnerloop(input, 'a')); system.out.println("string.repeat: " + usingstringrepeat(input, 'a')); } }

s: Reverse ONLY the alphabet characters in a string. Every special character stays exactly where it was.
x: reverse only letters reverseonlyletters.java package com.sdet.studyplan.medium; /** * problem: reverse only the alphabet characters in a string. every special * character stays exactly where it was. * * example: * input: "$%^&asdf@!lkj" * output: "$%^&jklf@!dsa" * * the letters in order are a s d f l k j. reversed they are j k l f d s a, * and those go back into the same letter positions. "$%^&" and "@!" never move. */ public class reverseonlyletters { /** * helper: is this character a letter? * * character.isletter does the job, but here it is written out so you can * see what it checks: a-z or a-z. */ public static boolean isletter(char ch) { return (ch >= 'a' && ch <= 'z') || (ch >= 'a' && ch <= 'z'); } /** * approach 1: pull the letters out, reverse them, put them back. * * three easy steps: * 1. loop the string and collect every letter into one string. * 2. loop that string backwards to reverse it. * 3. loop the original again. if the character is a letter, take the * next letter from the reversed string. if not, copy it as it is. * * the variable "next" remembers how many letters we have used so far. */ public static string usingreversedletters(string text) { string letters = ""; for (int i = 0; i < text.length(); i++) { char ch = text.charat(i); if (isletter(ch)) { letters = letters + ch; } } string reversed = ""; for (int i = letters.length() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { reversed = reversed + letters.charat(i); } string result = ""; int next = 0; for (int i = 0; i < text.length(); i++) { char ch = text.charat(i); if (isletter(ch)) { result = result + reversed.charat(next); next++; } else { result = result + ch; } } return result; } /** * approach 2: two positions, swapping from both ends. * * idea: "left" starts at the first character and "right" at the last. * if left is on a special character, move left forward. if right is on a * special character, move right back. only when both are on letters do we * swap them and move both. that way the special characters are never * touched. * * a string cannot be changed in place, so we work on a char array and * turn it back into a string at the end. */ public static string usingtwopointers(string text) { char[] ch = text.tochararray(); int left = 0; int right = ch.length - 1; while (left < right) { if (!isletter(ch[left])) { left++; } else if (!isletter(ch[right])) { right--; } else { char temp = ch[left]; ch[left] = ch[right]; ch[right] = temp; left++; right--; } } return new string(ch); } public static void main(string[] args) { string input = "$%^&asdf@!lkj"; system.out.println("input: " + input); system.out.println("reversed letters: " + usingreversedletters(input)); system.out.println("two pointers: " + usingtwopointers(input)); system.out.println(); system.out.println("no letters: " + usingtwopointers("$%^&@!")); system.out.println("all letters: " + usingtwopointers("abcdef")); system.out.println("with digits: " + usingtwopointers("a1b2c3")); } }

t: Reverse the last word in the sentence
s: Reverse only the LAST word of a sentence; every other word stays exactly where it is.
x: reverse the last word in the sentence reversethelastwordinthesentence.java package com.sdet.studyplan.medium; /** * problem: reverse only the last word of a sentence; every other word * stays exactly where it is. * * example: * input: "i am the chief" * output: "i am the feihc" */ public class reversethelastwordinthesentence { /** * approach 1: reverse the last word with a loop. * * idea: split the sentence into words, take the last element * (words[words.length - 1]), rebuild it character by character from * the end, and put it back in its slot. string.join() stitches the * sentence back together with spaces between the words. */ public static string usingloop(string sentence) { string[] words = sentence.split(" "); string lastword = words[words.length - 1]; stringbuilder reversed = new stringbuilder(); for (int i = lastword.length() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { reversed.append(lastword.charat(i)); } words[words.length - 1] = reversed.tostring(); // swap the last word in place return string.join(" ", words); } /** * approach 2: same plan, stringbuilder.reverse() shortcut. * * idea: identical split -> replace -> join flow, but the reversal * itself is the library one-liner. in real code you would write this * version; approach 1 exists so you understand what reverse() does. */ public static string usingstringbuilderreverse(string sentence) { string[] words = sentence.split(" "); int lastindex = words.length - 1; words[lastindex] = new stringbuilder(words[lastindex]).reverse().tostring(); return string.join(" ", words); } public static void main(string[] args) { string input = "i am the chief"; system.out.println("loop: " + usingloop(input)); system.out.println("stringbuilder: " + usingstringbuilderreverse(input)); } }

t: Reverse the string while preserving whitespace
s: Reverse a string, but every space must stay at its original index. Only the non-space characters get reversed.
x: reverse the string while preserving whitespace reversethestringwhilepreservingwhitespace.java package com.sdet.studyplan.medium; /** * problem: reverse a string, but every space must stay at its original * index. only the non-space characters get reversed. * * example: * input: "yu gan" (space at index 2) * output: "na guy" (letters y,u,g,a,n reversed to n,a,g,u,y; * the space never leaves index 2) */ public class reversethestringwhilepreservingwhitespace { /** * approach 1: reserve the spaces, then fill from the back. * * idea: two passes over a fresh char[]. * pass 1: copy each space into its original index, reserving it. * pass 2: walk the input left to right, and place each non-space * character into the result from the end, skipping reserved slots. * letters land in reverse order, spaces never move. */ public static string usingtwopasses(string text) { char[] chars = text.tochararray(); char[] result = new char[chars.length]; // pass 1: reserve the space positions. for (int i = 0; i < chars.length; i++) { if (chars[i] == ' ') { result[i] = ' '; } } // pass 2: fill letters from the back, hopping over reserved slots. int fill = chars.length - 1; for (int i = 0; i < chars.length; i++) { if (chars[i] != ' ') { if (result[fill] == ' ') { fill--; // skip the reserved space slot } result[fill] = chars[i]; fill--; } } return new string(result); // build a string out of a char[] } /** * approach 2: two pointers swapping towards the middle. * * idea: left and right pointers start at the two ends of a char[] * copy. each pointer skips over spaces on its side; when both point * at letters, swap them and step inwards. one pass, no second array. */ public static string usingtwopointers(string text) { char[] chars = text.tochararray(); int left = 0; int right = chars.length - 1; while (left < right) { if (chars[left] == ' ') { left++; // spaces stay put — walk past them } else if (chars[right] == ' ') { right--; } else { char temp = chars[left]; chars[left] = chars[right]; chars[right] = temp; left++; right--; } } return new string(chars); } public static void main(string[] args) { string input = "yu gan"; system.out.println("two passes: " + usingtwopasses(input)); system.out.println("two pointers: " + usingtwopointers(input)); } }

s: Rotate an array to the RIGHT by k positions — every element moves k steps to the right, and the ones that fall off the end wrap around to the front.
x: rotate array rotatearray.java package com.sdet.studyplan.medium; import java.util.arrays; /** * problem: rotate an array to the right by k positions — every element * moves k steps to the right, and the ones that fall off the end wrap * around to the front. * * example: * input: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], k = 3 * output: [5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4] * * java term worth learning: the % (modulo) operator wraps indexes around. * (i + k) % length always lands back inside the array, no matter how big * k is — that wrap-around is the rotation. */ public class rotatearray { /** * approach 1: place each element at its rotated index. * * idea: element at index i belongs at index (i + k) % length after * the rotation, so walk the input once and drop every value straight * into its final slot of a fresh array. * we also reduce k with k % length first: rotating by the array * length changes nothing, so k = 9 on a 7-element array is really * just k = 2. */ public static int[] usingextraarray(int[] nums, int k) { int n = nums.length; k = k % n; // rotating by n is a full circle -> same as rotating by 0 int[] rotated = new int[n]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { rotated[(i + k) % n] = nums[i]; } return rotated; } /** * approach 2: three reversals (the clever in-place trick). * * idea: rotating right by k is the same as: * 1. reverse the whole array [1,2,3,4,5,6,7] -> [7,6,5,4,3,2,1] * 2. reverse the first k items -> [5,6,7,4,3,2,1] * 3. reverse the remaining items -> [5,6,7,1,2,3,4] * no extra array needed. the helper reverses a section between two * indexes using the classic swap-the-ends loop. */ public static void usingthreereversals(int[] nums, int k) { int n = nums.length; k = k % n; reverse(nums, 0, n - 1); // step 1: whole array reverse(nums, 0, k - 1); // step 2: first k elements reverse(nums, k, n - 1); // step 3: the rest } /** reverse the elements of nums between indexes start and end (inclusive). */ private static void reverse(int[] nums, int start, int end) { while (start < end) { int temp = nums[start]; nums[start] = nums[end]; nums[end] = temp; start++; end--; } } public static void main(string[] args) { int[] input = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 }; int k = 3; system.out.println("extra array: " + arrays.tostring(usingextraarray(input, k))); int[] inplace = input.clone(); usingthreereversals(inplace, k); system.out.println("three reversals: " + arrays.tostring(inplace)); } }

s: Compress a string with RUN-LENGTH ENCODING — replace every run of repeated characters with the character followed by the run length.
x: string compression stringcompression.java package com.sdet.studyplan.medium; /** * problem: compress a string with run-length encoding — replace every run * of repeated characters with the character followed by the run length. * * example: * input: "aabbbcccddd" * output: "a2b3c3d3" */ public class stringcompression { /** * approach 1: compare with the previous character. * * idea: walk the string remembering the previous character and how * many times it has repeated. when the current character differs, * the run is over — write "previouschar + count" to the result and * restart the count. the final run has no "different" character after * it, so it is written once more after the loop. */ public static string usingpreviouschar(string text) { stringbuilder compressed = new stringbuilder(); char previous = text.charat(0); int count = 1; for (int i = 1; i < text.length(); i++) { char current = text.charat(i); if (current == previous) { count++; // run continues } else { compressed.append(previous).append(count); // run ended -> flush it previous = current; count = 1; } } compressed.append(previous).append(count); // flush the final run return compressed.tostring(); } /** * approach 2: two pointers — one marks the run, one finds its end. * * idea: "start" marks the first character of the current run. "scan" * runs ahead until it hits a different character (or the end of the * string). the run length is simply scan - start; write it, then jump * start to where scan stopped. same result, but you never carry a * separate "previous" variable. */ public static string usingtwopointers(string text) { stringbuilder compressed = new stringbuilder(); int start = 0; while (start < text.length()) { int scan = start; // move scan to the end of the current run of equal characters. while (scan < text.length() && text.charat(scan) == text.charat(start)) { scan++; } int runlength = scan - start; compressed.append(text.charat(start)).append(runlength); start = scan; // next run begins where this one ended } return compressed.tostring(); } public static void main(string[] args) { string input = "aabbbcccddd"; system.out.println("previous char: " + usingpreviouschar(input)); system.out.println("two pointers: " + usingtwopointers(input)); } }

s: Find all triplets — groups of three numbers — in an array that add up to a target.
x: triple sum triplesum.java package com.sdet.studyplan.medium; import java.util.hashset; import java.util.set; /** * problem: find all triplets — groups of three numbers — in an array that * add up to a target. * * example: * input: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], target = 6 * output: [1, 2, 3] * * note: with repeated values the same triplet can be reported more than * once; in a real task you would collect triplets into a set to dedupe. */ public class triplesum { /** * approach 1: three nested loops — try every combination. * * idea: one loop per slot of the triplet. j starts at i + 1 and k at * j + 1, so each combination is checked exactly once and no element * is used twice in the same triplet. */ public static void usingthreeloops(int[] nums, int target) { for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) { for (int j = i + 1; j < nums.length; j++) { for (int k = j + 1; k < nums.length; k++) { if (nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == target) { system.out.println("[" + nums[i] + ", " + nums[j] + ", " + nums[k] + "]"); } } } } } /** * approach 2: fix one number, then solve a twosum for the rest. * * idea: pick the first number with the outer loop. what remains is a * smaller question: "find two numbers after it that add up to * (target - first)" — and that is exactly the twosum problem, solved * here with the same hashset complement trick as in twosum. * recognizing that a big problem contains a smaller one you already * solved is the real lesson of this file. */ public static void usingtwosuminside(int[] nums, int target) { for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) { int first = nums[i]; int remainingtarget = target - first; // twosum over everything after index i. set<integer> seen = new hashset<>(); for (int j = i + 1; j < nums.length; j++) { int second = nums[j]; int complement = remainingtarget - second; if (seen.contains(complement)) { system.out.println("[" + first + ", " + complement + ", " + second + "]"); } seen.add(second); } } } public static void main(string[] args) { int[] input = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 }; int target = 6; system.out.println("three loops:"); usingthreeloops(input, target); system.out.println("twosum inside:"); usingtwosuminside(input, target); } }

s: Find all pairs of numbers in an array that add up to a target.
x: two sum twosum.java package com.sdet.studyplan.medium; import java.util.hashset; import java.util.set; /** * problem: find all pairs of numbers in an array that add up to a target. * * example: * input: [1, 4, 5, -1, 3], target = 4 * output: pairs [1, 3] and [5, -1] */ public class twosum { /** * approach 1: check every pair with nested loops. * * idea: for each number, try adding every number that comes after it * (j starts at i + 1, so we never repeat a pair or add a number to * itself). if the sum matches the target, we found a pair. */ public static void usingnestedloops(int[] nums, int target) { for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) { for (int j = i + 1; j < nums.length; j++) { if (nums[i] + nums[j] == target) { system.out.println("[" + nums[i] + ", " + nums[j] + "]"); } } } } /** * approach 2: remember what you have seen with a hashset. * * idea: for the current number, the partner it needs is * (target - number) — its complement. instead of scanning the array * for that partner, we ask the set "have i already seen the * complement?" set lookups are instant, so each number needs only one * question instead of a whole inner loop. */ public static void usinghashset(int[] nums, int target) { set<integer> seen = new hashset<>(); for (int num : nums) { int complement = target - num; // the partner this number needs if (seen.contains(complement)) { system.out.println("[" + complement + ", " + num + "]"); } seen.add(num); // remember this number for future lookups } } public static void main(string[] args) { int[] input = { 1, 4, 5, -1, 3 }; int target = 4; system.out.println("nested loops:"); usingnestedloops(input, target); system.out.println("hashset:"); usinghashset(input, target); } }

what is actually running this is the part most tutorials skip, and it explains nearly every strange thing selenium does later. your test is not "in" the browser. three separate programs are talking to each other. your testng test chromedriver chrome (a java process) ---> (a local server) ---> (the browser) http internal driver.findelement(by.id("name")) | +--> post /session/<id>/element {"using":"css selector","value":"#name"} <-- {"element-6066-...":"f3e2b1"} a reference, not the element selenium speaks the w3c webdriver protocol over http. three things follow from that picture, and each one saves you hours later: every single findelement is a round trip. a loop over a hundred rows makes a hundred network calls, which is why table loops feel slow. a webelement is a reference id the browser handed you, not a copy of the element. if the page redraws, that id points at nothing and you get staleelementreferenceexception . lesson 4 deals with it. chromedriver is a real operating-system process. something has to kill it, and that something is quit() .

s: The page is not ready and your test does not know it. This is the single biggest source of flaky UI tests, and "explain implicit versus explicit versus fluent" is close to guaranteed in an interview.
x: lesson 2 · waits lesson 02 · selenium waits the page is not ready and your test does not know it. this is the single biggest source of flaky ui tests, and "explain implicit versus explicit versus fluent" is close to guaranteed in an interview. every number on this page was measured on your machine, on selenium 4.21.0. the whole lesson in four lines 1. an implicit wait answers one question: is it in the dom yet? set once, applies to every findelement . 2. an explicit wait waits for a condition , at one point in the test. visible, clickable, text changed, anything. 3. fluent is an explicit wait with the polling and the ignored exceptions typed out by hand. webdriverwait is a fluentwait . 4. never mix implicit and explicit. measured below: asking for 6 seconds got 8.5. the problem modern pages load, then keep changing. an api call finishes and a table appears. a spinner clears and a button turns on. your test does not stop for any of that. findelement asks the browser once. if nothing matches, it throws nosuchelementexception straight away. driver.findelement(by.id("reveal")).click(); driver.findelement(by.id("delayed")); // throws. the element arrives 3s later. the obvious fix is thread.sleep(3000) . do not do it, and be ready to say why. it costs three seconds even when the element was ready in 200ms, and it still fails on the day the server is slow. it is both slower and less reliable than waiting properly. sleeps in a suite are the thing an interviewer is listening for. 1. implicit wait driver.manage().timeouts().implicitlywait(duration.ofseconds(10)); one line. set it once, and every findelement call for the rest of that driver's life will retry instead of failing immediately. the default is 0 . it is global, it is invisible at the call site, and it does exactly one thing: it retries until the element is in the dom. where it stops helping, and it fails silently the practice page has a button that is present from the first millisecond but disabled for two seconds. findelement returns it instantly, so a 10 second implicit wait never engages at all. then the click does nothing. chrome does not throw for a click on a disabled button. no exception, no error, nothing red. the test carries on and asserts against a page where the click never happened. i expected an elementnotinteractableexception when i wrote this test. there isn't one. that is worse, and it is the honest version of the story. so an implicit wait cannot wait for: visible, enabled, clickable, the text to change, an element to dis appear, or a count of rows. all of those are normal things to wait for. 2. explicit wait webdriverwait wait = new webdriverwait(driver, duration.ofseconds(10)); webelement delayed = wait.until( expectedconditions.visibilityofelementlocated(by.id("delayed"))); this waits for a named condition , at one point in the test. it polls every 500 milliseconds, and it swallows notfoundexception while it polls so a missing element is not an error yet. if the condition never comes true it throws timeoutexception . the two cases the implicit wait could not touch: wait.until(expectedconditions.elementtobeclickable(by.id("later"))).click(); wait.until(expectedconditions.texttobe(by.id("status"), "complete")); conditions worth being able to name out loud: condition waits until presenceofelementlocated it is in the dom. may still be hidden. visibilityofelementlocated in the dom and displayed. elementtobeclickable visible and enabled. texttobe the element's text equals what you said. invisibilityofelementlocated it has gone, or hidden. the spinner case. alertispresent a native alert has opened. numberofelementstobe the locator matches exactly n things. presence versus visibility is a real interview follow-up. presence is satisfied by an element with display:none , and then your gettext() returns an empty string and the assertion fails somewhere confusing. reach for visibility unless you have a reason not to. 3. fluent wait wait<webdriver> wait = new fluentwait<>(driver) .withtimeout(duration.ofseconds(10)) .pollingevery(duration.ofmillis(250)) .ignoring(nosuchelementexception.class); webelement delayed = wait.until(d -> d.findelement(by.id("delayed"))); three knobs: how long, how often, and which exceptions to swallow while polling. the line that makes this question easy webdriverwait extends fluentwait . i checked the bytecode in selenium-support-4.21.0.jar on this machine: its constructor calls withtimeout(yourduration) , then pollingevery(500ms) , then ignoring(notfoundexception.class) . so they are not two mechanisms. fluent is the general one; webdriverwait is the same object with sensible defaults already filled in. say that and you have answered better than someone reciting three bullet points. which means you only reach for fluentwait when you want to change one of those defaults. polling a slow, expensive condition less often. or ignoring staleelementreferenceexception on a table that rerenders underneath you, which is the classic real use. 4. why you must not mix them the selenium documentation says it flatly: do not mix implicit and explicit waits. doing so can cause unpredictable wait times. for example, setting an implicit wait of 10 seconds and an explicit wait of 15 seconds could cause a timeout to occur after 20 seconds. that is a claim, so i measured it. two tests, same missing element, same 6 second explicit wait. one has a 4 second implicit wait set, the other has none. explicit only: explicit 6s timed out after 6183ms mixed waits: implicit 4s + explicit 6s timed out after 8526ms you asked for six seconds and got eight and a half. stable across runs, within about 50ms. why. the explicit wait polls by calling findelement . once an implicit wait is set, each of those polls now blocks for up to four seconds on its own. a poll that starts just before the six second deadline still has to run to completion. so your real timeout is the explicit timeout plus up to one implicit wait, and nobody reading the test can see it. the rule. pick one. in practice: leave the implicit wait at 0 , never set it, and use explicit waits everywhere. that is what a framework does, and it is the answer to "which do you use and why". check yourself what is the only question an implicit wait can answer? has this element finished loading fully is this element ready to be clicked is this element in the dom yet you click a button that is present but disabled . what does selenium throw? elementnotinteractableexception, straight away nothing at all, the click vanishes timeoutexception once the wait expires how is webdriverwait related to fluentwait does it time out? at six seconds, the explicit wait wins later than six, they add together at four seconds, the implicit wait wins why prefer visibilityofelementlocated over presenceofelementlocated ? this order. what it means , in one line and in your own words. where it is in my framework , naming a class. what it buys me , the problem it removes. definition alone sounds memorised. definition plus a place sounds like you have used it. 1. abstraction what it means. show what something does. hide how it does it. where it lives, one: webdriver itself. you have been using abstraction since lesson 1 without calling it that. webdriver driver = new chromedriver(options); webdriver is an interface. it declares get , findelement , quit . it contains no code that drives a browser. chromedriver supplies that. your variable is the interface type, so the rest of the test cannot tell which browser it has. where it lives, two: the page object. this is the one to lead with. // the test says what the user does. loginpage.loginas("yugan", "secret"); // the page object owns how it is done. public homepage loginas(string user, string pass) { type(username, user); type(password, pass); click(submit); return new homepage(driver); } what it buys you. the login form gets redesigned. one method changes. the forty tests that log in do not. 2. encapsulation what it means. keep the data private. let people reach it only through methods you control. people confuse this with abstraction constantly, so have the distinction ready. abstraction hides complexity. encapsulation protects state. abstraction is a design idea; encapsulation is the private keyword doing a job. where it lives: the driver manager. public final class drivermanager { private static final threadlocal<webdriver> driver = new threadlocal<>(); public static webdriver getdriver() { return driver.get(); } public static void set(webdriver driver) { driver.set(driver); } public static void unload() { if (driver.get() != null) { driver.get().quit(); driver.remove(); // nobody can forget this now } } } the threadlocal is private . no test can touch it. that is what makes the remove() impossible to forget, which is the leak you saw in testng lesson 6. also here: locators in a page object are private static final by , never public. a test that could read loginpage.username would start doing its own findelement , and the abstraction would rot within a month. the one-rule version, worth saying out loud "nothing in my tests package imports selenium. no by , no webelement , no webdriver . if a test needs one, my page object is missing a method." that single sentence demonstrates encapsulation, abstraction and design taste at once. 3. inheritance what it means. a class takes on the fields and methods of a parent, so shared code is written once. where it lives, one: basetest . every test class extends it, so the browser lifecycle is written once instead of forty times. public abstract class basetest { @beforemethod(alwaysrun = true) public void startbrowser() { drivermanager.set(driverfactory.create(config.browser())); } @aftermethod(alwaysrun = true) public void stopbrowser() { drivermanager.unload(); } } public class logintest extends basetest { ... } where it lives, two: basepage , holding the driver, the wait, and the shared click and type helpers that every page needs. what it buys you. one place to change how every test starts a browser. one place that owns every wait in the framework. the follow-up they ask next: composition over inheritance inheritance is for "is a". a logintest is a test. a loginpage is a page. fine. a header, a nav bar or a modal is not a page, and it appears on twenty pages. do not inherit it. compose it: the page holds one as a field. public class homepage extends basepage { public final header header = new header(driver); // composed, not inherited } deep inheritance chains are the classic framework smell. two levels is plenty. 4. polymorphism what it means. one name, many behaviours. it comes in two kinds and you should name both. runtime polymorphism (overriding) the reference type is fixed at compile time. the object behind it is decided while running. this is how cross-browser works , and it is the best example you have. public static webdriver create(browser browser) { switch (browser) { case the compiler picks. protected void click(by locator) { click(locator, config.defaulttimeout()); } protected void click(by locator, duration timeout) { ... } overloading overriding same method name yes layer its one job key piece 1 configuration no value is hard-coded layered properties, -d wins 2 driver make a browser, safely, in parallel driverfactory + threadlocal 3 pages hide the dom from the tests page objects, basepage 4 data test data lives outside the code excel via poi, @dataprovider 5 tests read like the user's journey testng, basetest , groups 6 reporting diagnose a failure without rerunning listeners, screenshots, retry, allure layers 1 and 2 are setup. layer 3 is where the design taste shows. layer 6 is what separates a framework from a folder of tests. the one rule that ties them together say this sentence and stop talking for a second "nothing in my tests package imports selenium. no by , no webelement , no webdriver . if a test needs one, my page object is missing a method." it is short, it is checkable, and most candidates cannot say it about their own repo. selenium's own guidance agrees: page objects "should seldom expose the underlying webdriver instance". the 90 second script, honest version four beats. do not memorise the words, memorise the four beats and the one number in each. beat 1 — where you actually are (about 15 seconds) "i have built the testng side of a framework in my own practice repo, and i am building the selenium layer on top of it now. so let me tell you what is running today, and then how i am putting the rest together." that is one sentence and it buys you the whole rest of the answer. you are now describing, not claiming. beat 2 — what is running today (about 30 seconds) "testng driving it, with suite xmls for selection. tests tagged into groups so the pre-merge run is the smoke slice and the nightly is everything. data comes out of excel through apache poi into a @dataprovider — i wrote that reader, and i found a bug in it where a blank row in the middle of a sheet silently dropped every row after it, because it used getphysicalnumberofrows instead of getlastrownum . parallel execution with a threadlocal , and a listener layer with a retry analyser." all of that is true and all of it is yours. the poi bug is the strongest thing in the answer, because nobody invents a debugging story that specific. beat 3 — the selenium design (about 30 seconds) "the selenium layer is a driver factory returning chrome, firefox or edge behind the webdriver interface, held in a threadlocal so a parallel run cannot cross the streams. page objects with plain by constants and explicit waits, not pagefactory . explicit waits everywhere and the implicit wait left at zero, because mixing them makes the timeout unpredictable — i measured that: a four second implicit wait plus a six second explicit wait timed out at eight and a half seconds." that measurement is your credibility. it is a number from your own machine. beat 4 — failures (about 15 seconds) "on failure the listener takes a screenshot and logs the url, the browser and the data row, so i can diagnose without rerunning. retry is deliberate and maven, pinned versions in one properties block, one test that opens a browser and asserts a title. why first: it proves the setup on a clean machine before any design decisions can hide a broken build. config. layered. a checked-in default, an environment file, then -d on the command line beating both. why early: every layer after this wants a url, a browser and a timeout, and if you do not build it now you will scatter system.getproperty through the whole codebase. no secrets in the repo, ever. driver factory and driver manager. a browser enum, per-browser options, and a threadlocal<webdriver> behind a private field. why here: parallel safety is impossible to retrofit. bolt it on later and you rewrite every page object. page objects. a basepage owning the driver and every wait, then one page object per page, plus components for the header and modals that appear everywhere. enforce the no-selenium-in-tests rule from the first page object, not from the fiftieth. data layer. poi wrapped so tests never touch a poi type, rows mapped to objects, wired into @dataprovider . why wrapped: the day you move from excel to csv or a database, one class changes. listeners guidance never mentions it, and its lazy proxies compose badly with explicit waits. plain by constants are clearer. how do you handle waits? explicit everywhere, implicit left at zero. mixing them makes the timeout the explicit one plus up to one implicit wait. how do you do cross-browser? a factory returning three drivers behind the webdriver interface. one config value changes; no test or page object knows. how do you manage drivers? selenium manager. built in since 4.6, so no webdrivermanager and no system.setproperty . how do you handle flaky tests? find the real cause first, usually a wait. iretryanalyzer for genuinely non-deterministic ones, and the retry is visible in the report, never silent. which reporting tool? allure. extentreports was sunset by its own author, and allure x: the follow-ups, and one line each they ask you say why threadlocal ? two threads share one instance, so they share a plain field and one overwrites the other. threadlocal gives each thread its own driver. why not pagefactory ? selenium's own page object guidance never mentions it, and its lazy proxies compose badly with explicit waits. plain by constants are clearer. how do you handle waits? explicit everywhere, implicit left at zero. mixing them makes the timeout the explicit one plus up to one implicit wait. how do you do cross-browser? a factory returning three drivers behind the webdriver interface. one config value changes; no test or page object knows. how do you manage drivers? selenium manager. built in since 4.6, so no webdrivermanager and no system.setproperty . how do you handle flaky tests? find the real cause first, usually a wait. iretryanalyzer for genuinely non-deterministic ones, and the retry is visible in the report, never silent. which reporting tool? allure. extentreports was sunset by its own author, and allure survives a change of test runner. how do you check five things in one test? softassert , then assertall() . a hard assert stops at the first failure and hides the other four. how is data separated? excel through poi, wrapped so tests never see a poi type, into a @dataprovider . a non-programmer can add a row. what is staleelementreference ? you found the element, then the page replaced it. the handle points at a node no longer in the dom. re-find it; a longer wait does not help. three answers that lose you the room "we use thread.sleep where it's flaky." slower and less reliable than waiting properly. this is the single thing interviewers listen for. "we use extentreports." fine to have used it, but know it was sunset by its own author. naming it as a current choice dates you. "we use webdrivermanager." unnecessary since selenium 4.6. same problem: it says you learned from tutorials written in 2019.

check yourself you are asked about your framework and you have built part of one. what do you open with? describe the full thing as yours say you have not built one yet say what runs, then the design why build the threadlocal driver manager early rather than later? retrofitting it rewrites every page object because parallel runs are much faster because selenium manager requires it first one test needs to check five fields on a confirmation page. how? five separate tests, one per field softassert, then call assertall five asserts, and read the first a test throws staleelementreferenceexception . what happened? the element never appeared on the page the wait timed out before it loaded the page replaced it after you found it

tonight say the four beats out loud, timed. ninety seconds. if you run over, cut beat 3, not beat 2, because beat 2 is the part that is provably yours. cover the right column of the follow-up table and work down the left. any you cannot answer in one sentence, ask me now. reread the two numbers you own: the mixed-wait measurement from lesson 2 , and the poi getphysicalnumberofrows bug. those two are what make the rest sound like experience rather than reading. primary source selenium's page object models is the one to have read, and it is short. it is where the "seldom expose the underlying webdriver instance" rule comes from, and where page methods returning page objects is recommended. where the design comes from framework-brief.md, the spec for the framework you start building on monday. every design claim in this lesson is from there, so the answers you give tomorrow are the thing you will actually build. stuck? ask me tonight, and nothing is too small. worth asking: "what if they ask how many tests are in my suite?" there is an honest answer to that one and it is better than a number you have to defend. ← lesson 3 framework brief lesson 5 →

x: lesson 5 · exception handling lesson 05 · selenium exception handling two halves. the java rules, which they will ask you cold. then the selenium catalogue: what each one means, why it happened, and the fix. every exception below is thrown for real by a test in this repo, and the class hierarchy was read out of the jar rather than remembered. the whole lesson in four lines 1. checked means the compiler forces you to deal with it. unchecked means it does not. 2. every selenium exception is unchecked. that is deliberate, and it is why tests let them fly. 3. in a test, catching an exception usually turns a real failure into a false pass. let it propagate. 4. the five you must know by sight: nosuchelement , timeout , staleelementreference , elementnotinteractable , elementclickintercepted . part one: the java rules checked versus unchecked the whole distinction is one question: does the compiler force you to handle it? throwable ├── error jvm-level. outofmemoryerror. do not catch these. └── exception ├── runtimeexception unchecked. nullpointer, illegalargument, ... │ compiler says nothing. └── everything else checked. ioexception, sqlexception, ... compiler forces try/catch or throws. the line to say: "checked exceptions are conditions a caller could reasonably recover from, so the compiler makes them part of the signature. unchecked ones are programming errors, and forcing everyone to catch them would just produce empty catch blocks." try, catch, finally try { // work that might fail } catch (ioexception e) { // handle it, or rethrow with context } finally { // runs whether or not it threw. cleanup goes here. } finally runs even when the try block returns. that is what makes it the place for cleanup. in a test framework, though, cleanup belongs in @aftermethod(alwaysrun = true) , which is testng's version of the same idea. throw versus throws throw is a statement. it throws one object, right now. throws is part of a method signature. it declares what might come out. interviewers ask this to check you are not guessing. public row read(int i) throws ioexception { // declares if (i < 0) throw new illegalargumentexception("row " + i); // throws } custom exceptions, and when they earn their place public class frameworkexception extends runtimeexception { public frameworkexception(string message, throwable cause) { super(message, cause); // keep the cause. always. } } worth it when you can add context the original could not carry. "could not read row 7 of palindrome-data.xlsx" beats a bare ioexception . extend runtimeexception so it does not pollute every signature above it, and always pass the cause through, or you throw away the stack trace that tells you what really happened. the part that matters for testing a catch block in a test is usually a bug // never do this. try { driver.findelement(by.id("submit")).click(); } catch (exception e) { system.out.println("could not click"); } the button was missing. the application is broken. and your test just printed a line nobody reads and passed green . a test's job is to fail when the application is wrong. swallowing the exception is the one way to guarantee it cannot do its job. so how do you assert that something should fail? not with a catch block. declare it: @test(expectedexceptions = nosuchelementexception.class) public void nosuchelement() { driver.findelement(by.id("does-not-exist")); } that test passes because the exception was thrown, and fails if it is not. the intent is in the signature where a reader sees it. where catching is legitimate, and be ready to name these, because "never catch anything" is not a real answer: in the framework, not the test. a basepage helper that retries a click once on elementclickinterceptedexception . to add context, then rethrow. catch, wrap in your own exception with the row number and the url, throw that. never swallow. in an @aftermethod . teardown that throws hides the real failure with a second one. in a listener. a screenshot that fails must not take the report down with it. part two: the selenium catalogue read out of selenium-api-4.21.0.jar with javap , not from memory: runtimeexception └── webdriverexception three things that diagram tells you, and most people miss all three 1. webdriverexception extends runtimeexception , so every selenium exception is unchecked. the compiler never forces a catch. that is a design decision: a broken locator is a programming error, not something the caller recovers from. 2. elementclickintercepted extends elementnotinteractable . so catching the parent silently catches the child, and you swallow the cookie-banner bug you were hunting. 3. webdriverwait ignores notfoundexception , which covers nosuchelement . but staleelementreference sits on a different branch, so it is not ignored. a wait over a rerendering element blows up unless you say .ignoring(staleelementreferenceexception.class) . that is the real reason fluentwait exists. the five you must know by sight exception what happened the fix nosuchelementexception nothing matched the locator, right now. check the locator first, it is usually a typo. then check you are on the right page or inside the right frame. then add an explicit wait. timeoutexception the locator may be fine. the condition never came true in time. ask whether you waited for the right condition. waiting for presence when you needed visibility is the usual cause. staleelementreferenceexception you found it, then the page replaced that node. your handle points at something the dom threw away. re-find it. a longer wait cannot help, because the wait already succeeded once. do not store webelement fields on a page object. elementnotinteractableexception it is in the dom but cannot receive input. hidden, zero-sized, or off screen. elementtobeclickable , or scroll it into view. check it is not display:none . elementclickinterceptedexception something is on top of it. a cookie banner, a modal, a spinner. wait for the overlay to go with invisibilityofelementlocated . dismiss the banner. a js click hides the problem rather than fixing it. the rest, one line each invalidselectorexception the selector is malformed. classic cause: xpath passed to by.cssselector . noalertpresentexception you switched to an alert that is not open. wait for alertispresent . nosuchwindowexception the handle you switched to is closed. re-read getwindowhandles() . nosuchframeexception wrong frame name or index. remember to switchto().defaultcontent() on the way out. sessionnotcreatedexception the browser never started. usually a browser and driver version mismatch. webdriverexception the catch-all parent. seeing this raw usually means the session died. the one that throws nothing at all clicking a disabled button raises no exception. exception is the good case. it is the silent no-op that ruins your afternoon. staleelementreference, the one they probe it is the favourite follow-up because it catches people who learned exceptions from a list. the trap: it sounds like a timing problem, so people add a longer wait, and it keeps happening. webelement row = driver.findelement(by.cssselector("#list .row")); row.gettext(); // fine s: Eight ways to find an element. You will use two of them. This lesson covers all eight quickly, then spends its time on CSS and XPath, which is where the real skill is. Every selector on this page ran
x: lesson 6 · locators lesson 06 · selenium locators eight ways to find an element. you will use two of them. this lesson covers all eight quickly, then spends its time on css and xpath, which is where the real skill is. every selector on this page ran green in locatorstest . the whole lesson in four lines 1. eight by strategies exist. in practice you use cssselector and xpath , plus id when the page is kind. 2. css is shorter and reads better. use it by default. 3. xpath does two things css cannot: match on visible text , and walk up the tree. 4. a good locator describes what the thing is , not where it sits . the eight strategies strategy example when by.id by.id("email") always, if the page gives you one. fastest and clearest. by.name by.name("emailaddress") form fields. common and reasonably stable. by.classname by.classname("field") rarely. see the trap below. by.tagname by.tagname("li") counting things. almost never for targeting one. by.linktext by.linktext("read the terms and conditions") links, whole text, exact match. by.partiallinktext by.partiallinktext("terms and") links where part of the text is dynamic. by.cssselector by.cssselector("[data-testid='submit']") your default. most things. by.xpath by.xpath("//li[text()='enterprise']") text matching, and going up the tree. the trap everybody hits once by.classname takes one class name, not a list. an element with class="plan featured" is not found by by.classname("plan featured") . when you need both, use css: by.cssselector(".plan.featured") . that is most of why by.classname is rarely worth using. css, the syntax worth memorising seven forms cover nearly everything. syntax means example #id that id #email .class that class .plan .a.b both classes .plan.featured [attr='v'] attribute equals [data-testid='submit'] a > b direct child only #plans > li a b descendant, any depth #users td :nth-child(n) position, 1-based #plans li:nth-child(2) three more for partial attribute matching, which is how you survive generated values: [data-testid^='pass'] starts with [data-testid$='input'] ends with [class*='ui-'] contains xpath, and the two things only it can do the everyday form looks like a path: //input[@name='password'] any input with that name, anywhere //*[contains(@class,'ui-')] any element whose class contains that (//li[@class='plan'])[1] the first match, 1-based note // means "anywhere in the document" and / means "direct child". those are the css a b and a > b in different clothes. the answer to "why would you ever use xpath?" 1. it can match visible text. css has no way to do this at all. //li[text()='enterprise'] 2. it can walk up the tree. css only ever goes downwards. xpath can go up and then back down. //td[text()='bob']/parent::tr/td[3] find bob, go up to his row, read column 3 those two are the whole case for xpath. everything else css does more neatly. row scoping, the pattern you will use most real applications are full of tables and lists. you almost never want "the third row". you want "the row for chandra". that is one xpath shape, and it is worth being able to write from memory: //tr[td[text()='chandra']]/td[2] the row containing chandra, then its 2nd cell read it as: find a tr that has a td with this text, then take its second td . the outer brackets are a filter, not a position. what makes a locator survive a redesign this is the part interviewers actually care about, and it is a design question rather than a syntax one. the rule a good locator describes what the element is . a bad one describes where it currently sits . layout changes every sprint. identity does not. prefer avoid why #email /html/body/div[2]/form/input[1] an absolute path breaks when anyone adds a wrapper div. [data-testid='submit'] .btn-primary-9f3a2b generated class names change on every build. //tr[td[text()='bob']] #users tr:nth-child(2) row 2 becomes row 3 the moment data changes. one clear attribute five chained conditions the longer the locator, the more ways it can break. the best answer of all, and worth saying out loud: ask the developers for a data-testid . an attribute that exists only for testing cannot be broken by a redesign, because nothing else uses it. framing it as a conversation with the dev team rather than a locator trick is what makes it a senior answer. relative locators, a selenium 4 addition import static org.openqa.selenium.support.locators.relativelocator.with; driver.findelement(with(by.tagname("input")).torightof(by.id("city-label"))); also above , below , toleftof and near . genuinely useful when the only stable thing on the page is the label next to the field you want. worth naming in an interview because it shows you know selenium 4 and not just selenium 2. findelement versus findelements findelement returns one. throws nosuchelementexception if there are none. findelements returns a list . returns an empty list if there are none. never throws. that difference is a common question. it also gives you the idiom for "check something is absent", which cannot be done with findelement without catching an exception: assert.asserttrue(driver.findelements(by.cssselector(".error")).isempty()); check yourself what can xpath do that css cannot? match attributes and partial attributes select by position within a parent match text, and move up the tree why does by.classname("plan featured") fail? it accepts only one class name class names cannot contain spaces it needs a dot before each name what does findelements return when nothing matches? null, which you must check for an empty list, and no exception nosuchelementexception, immediately why is /html/body/div[2]/form/input[1] a bad locator? absolute xpath is much slower to run xpath should never start at html it breaks when the layout changes you need bob's status cell, and rows reorder. what is the shape? t: XPath, and the two things only it can do
x: xpath, and the two things only it can do the everyday form looks like a path: //input[@name='password'] any input with that name, anywhere //*[contains(@class,'ui-')] any element whose class contains that (//li[@class='plan'])[1] the first match, 1-based note // means "anywhere in the document" and / means "direct child". those are the css a b and a > b in different clothes. the answer to "why would you ever use xpath?" 1. it can match visible text. css has no way to do this at all. //li[text()='enterprise'] 2. it can walk up the tree. css only ever goes downwards. xpath can go up and then back down. //td[text()='bob']/parent::tr/td[3] find bob, go up to his row, read column 3 those two are the whole case for xpath. everything else css does more neatly. row scoping, the pattern you will use most real applications are full of tables and lists. you almost never want "the third row". you want "the row for chandra". that is one xpath shape, and it is worth being able to write from memory: //tr[td[text()='chandra']]/td[2] the row containing chandra, then its 2nd cell read it as: find a tr that has a td with this text, then take its second td . the outer brackets are a filter, not a position.

t: What makes a locator survive a redesign
x: what makes a locator survive a redesign this is the part interviewers actually care about, and it is a design question rather than a syntax one. the rule a good locator describes what the element is . a bad one describes where it currently sits . layout changes every sprint. identity does not. prefer avoid why #email /html/body/div[2]/form/input[1] an absolute path breaks when anyone adds a wrapper div. [data-testid='submit'] .btn-primary-9f3a2b generated class names change on every build. //tr[td[text()='bob']] #users tr:nth-child(2) row 2 becomes row 3 the moment data changes. one clear attribute five chained conditions the longer the locator, the more ways it can break. the best answer of all, and worth saying out loud: ask the developers for a data-testid . an attribute that exists only for testing cannot be broken by a redesign, because nothing else uses it. framing it as a conversation with the dev team rather than a locator trick is what makes it a senior answer. relative locators, a selenium 4 addition import static org.openqa.selenium.support.locators.relativelocator.with; driver.findelement(with(by.tagname("input")).torightof(by.id("city-label"))); also above , below , toleftof and near . genuinely useful when the only stable thing on the page is the label next to the field you want. worth naming in an interview because it shows you know selenium 4 and not just selenium 2.

findelement versus findelements findelement returns one. throws nosuchelementexception if there are none. findelements returns a list . returns an empty list if there are none. never throws. that difference is a common question. it also gives you the idiom for "check something is absent", which cannot be done with findelement without catching an exception: assert.asserttrue(driver.findelements(by.cssselector(".error")).isempty());

check yourself what can xpath do that css cannot? match attributes and partial attributes select by position within a parent match text, and move up the tree why does by.classname("plan featured") fail? it accepts only one class name class names cannot contain spaces it needs a dot before each name what does findelements return when nothing matches? null, which you must check for an empty list, and no exception nosuchelementexception, immediately why is /html/body/div[2]/form/input[1] a bad locator? absolute xpath is much slower to run xpath should never start at html it breaks when the layout changes you need bob's status cell, and rows reorder. what is the shape? filter the row by text, then pick the cell take the second row, then the third cell read every cell and search the results

run it mvn test -dsurefire.suitexmlfiles=selenium.xml -dtest=locatorstest eight tests, green as shipped. locatorstest.java has every selector on this page as a live assertion, so if you want to check a form works, change it there and rerun.

practise open src/test/resources/pages/lesson4.html in chrome. press f12, and in the console try $$("your selector here") . it returns the matches instantly, which is the tightest feedback loop there is for building a locator. use $x("your xpath") for xpath. write a locator for chandra's role cell three ways: by css position, by xpath position, and by xpath row filter. then say which one you would put in a framework and why. primary source selenium's locator strategies for the eight, and mdn's css selectors reference for the syntax. mdn is the better source for css than any selenium tutorial. files this lesson uses locatorstest.java and src/test/resources/pages/lesson4.html , both new and in selenium.xml . eight tests, verified green. stuck? ask me. worth asking: "is xpath really slower than css?" it is repeated everywhere and the honest answer is more interesting than the claim. ← lesson 5 mission lesson 7 →

interviewers ask about. this lesson is those five, plus tables and the javascript escape hatch. all of it ran green in elementtypestest . the whole lesson in one box ordinary elements: click() , sendkeys() , gettext() , clear() , isdisplayed() , isenabled() , isselected() , getattribute() . the five exceptions to that: <select> needs the select class. alerts need switchto().alert() . frames need switchto().frame() , and switching back out. new tabs need window handles. hover needs the actions class. 1. dropdowns only for a real <select> tag. wrap the element, then choose. select country = new select(driver.findelement(by.id("country"))); country.selectbyvisibletext("united kingdom"); // what the user sees country.selectbyvalue("us"); // the value attribute country.selectbyindex(0); // 0-based country.getfirstselectedoption().gettext(); // read it back country.getoptions().size(); // all options country.ismultiple(); multi-select adds the other half: skills.getallselectedoptions(); skills.deselectbyvalue("java"); skills.deselectall(); // throws on a single select the follow-up: what if it is not a <select>? most modern dropdowns are divs styled to look like a dropdown. the select class throws unexpectedtagnameexception on those. then it is just clicking. click the toggle, wait for the options to be visible, click the one you want. say this in an interview and you have shown you have tested a real application rather than a tutorial page. 2. checkboxes and radios click() toggles. it does not tick. calling click() on a box that is already ticked unticks it . every framework ends up with this helper, and writing it out is a good interview answer. private void setchecked(webelement box, boolean wanted) { if (box.isselected() != wanted) { box.click(); } } isselected() is the one that reads checked state. do not use getattribute("checked") , which reports the original html rather than the current state. radios work the same way, except clicking one clears the others in its group automatically. you never need to unclick a radio. 3. alerts a browser alert is not part of the page. no locator can reach it. you switch to it. alert alert = wait.until(expectedconditions.alertispresent()); alert.gettext(); alert.accept(); // ok alert.dismiss(); // cancel alert.sendkeys("yugan"); // only for a prompt type buttons can you type? alert() ok only no confirm() ok and cancel no prompt() ok and cancel yes leave an alert open and every following command throws unhandledalertexception . always accept or dismiss it. a native alert is the browser's own dialog. a "modal" built out of html is not an alert at all, and you locate it normally. knowing that distinction is the point of the question. 4. frames an element inside an iframe is invisible to the driver until you switch in. not slow to find. invisible. you get nosuchelementexception and it looks like a locator problem. driver.switchto().frame("theframe"); // by name or id driver.switchto().frame(0); // by index driver.switchto().frame(element); // by webelement // ... work inside ... driver.switchto().defaultcontent(); // back to the top document driver.switchto().parentframe(); // up one level only the switch back out is the half people forget. everything after it fails, and the failure appears somewhere unrelated to the frame. 5. windows and tabs opening a new tab does not move the driver. it keeps talking to the old one until you switch. string original = driver.getwindowhandle(); // save where you are driver.findelement(by.id("new-tab")).click(); wait.until(expectedconditions.numberofwindowstobe(2)); for (string handle : driver.getwindowhandles()) { if (!handle.equals(original)) { driver.switchto().window(handle); } } // ... work in the new tab ... driver.close(); // closes this tab only driver.switchto().window(original); // you must switch back a handle is an opaque id string, not a title or a url. and close() versus quit() matters here: close() shuts one tab, quit() ends the whole session and kills the driver process. 6. actions: hover, drag, right click webelement has no hover method. actions is the only way. new actions(driver) .movetoelement(menu) // hover .perform(); // nothing happens until perform() new actions(driver).contextclick(row).perform(); // right click new actions(driver).doubleclick(cell).perform(); new actions(driver).draganddrop(source, target).perform(); new actions(driver).keydown(keys.shift).click(item).keyup(keys.shift).perform(); the one rule: nothing runs until perform() . a chain without it is a silent no-op, and it is the classic actions bug. 7. tables a table is just nested elements. two things you actually do: // count rows test starts checking the wrong customer while still passing. 8. the javascript escape hatch ((javascriptexecutor) driver) .executescript("arguments[0].scrollintoview({block:'center'});", element); sendkeys with the option text why is a javascript click usually the wrong fix for a failing click? it is much slower than a normal click it does not work in headless chrome it hides a bug a real user x: lesson 8 · screenshots lesson 08 · selenium screenshots short lesson, and the one where the two courses meet. testng lesson 7 told you ontestfailure is where the screenshot goes. this is the other half: what actually takes it, and why the listener cannot reach your driver unless you have built for it. all measured on this machine. the whole lesson in four lines 1. cast the driver to takesscreenshot , then getscreenshotas(...) . 2. three output types: file to save, bytes to attach to a report, base64 to embed in html. 3. file gives you a temp file. copy it or you lose it. 4. put it in a listener, not in your tests. one class covers every test in the suite. taking one takesscreenshot is a separate interface from webdriver , so you cast: file temp = ((takesscreenshot) driver).getscreenshotas(outputtype.file); all the browser drivers implement it. the cast is safe in practice, and it is why the line looks odd the first time you see it. the three output types type you get use it for outputtype.file a file in the temp directory saving to disk yourself outputtype.bytes byte[] attaching to allure or a report, in memory outputtype.base64 string embedding straight into an html report the bug everyone hits: "my screenshots disappeared" outputtype.file returns a file in the system temp directory. it is deleted when the jvm exits. if you keep the file reference and never copy the bytes anywhere, you have nothing after the run. file temp = ((takesscreenshot) driver).getscreenshotas(outputtype.file); files.createdirectories(out.getparent()); files.copy(temp.topath(), out, standardcopyoption.replace_existing); // this line older tutorials use fileutils.copyfile from apache commons io. that works, but it is a whole dependency for one line that java.nio.file.files already does. element screenshots, a selenium 4 addition since selenium 4, webelement implements takesscreenshot too. you can capture one component instead of the whole viewport, which makes a report much easier to read. webelement table = driver.findelement(by.id("users")); file justthetable = table.getscreenshotas(outputtype.file); measured on this page: the full viewport came out at 50,012 bytes and the single table at 9,130 bytes . the test asserts that relationship rather than describing it. worth knowing for a follow-up: a plain selenium screenshot captures the viewport , not the whole scrollable page. full-page capture is not part of the w3c webdriver standard, so it needs a browser-specific command or a scroll-and-stitch helper. saying that is a better answer than assuming it grabs everything. where it actually belongs never in your tests. you would write the same six lines four hundred times, and every test would carry code about diagnosing itself. one listener covers the whole suite: public class screenshotlistener implements itestlistener { @override public void ontestfailure(itestresult result) { webdriver driver = drivermanager.get(); if (driver == null) return; // @beforemethod may have failed try { file temp = ((takesscreenshot) driver).getscreenshotas(outputtype.file); files.createdirectories(out); files.copy(temp.topath(), out.resolve(name), replace_existing); } catch (ioexception | runtimeexception e) { // swallowed on purpose, see below } } } attach it with @listeners(screenshotlistener.class) on the class, or in testng.xml for the whole suite. the design point, and it is the best thing in this lesson a listener is handed an itestresult . it cannot see a private webdriver field on your test class. so the driver has to live somewhere both can reach. that is drivermanager , and it is the practical reason the class exists, before you even get to thread safety. say this in an interview and you have connected your listener design to your driver design in one sentence. most people describe them as two unrelated features. three details that make it production code null-check the driver. if @beforemethod failed, there is no browser. a listener that throws here replaces your real failure with a nullpointerexception from the listener, which is a genuinely horrible thing to debug. swallow exceptions, and only here. this is the exception to lesson 5's rule. a screenshot that fails must not take down the report. it is diagnostics, not the test. name the file so it is findable. class, method and a timestamp: screenshottest.thisonefailswhenyoufliptheconstant-20260829-164835-309.png the timestamp matters because a retried test writes twice, and a fixed name would overwrite the first attempt, which is usually the interesting one. the gotcha from testng lesson 7, and it still applies a retried attempt fires ontestskipped , not ontestfailure . so a screenshot listener that only implements ontestfailure captures nothing for the attempts you most want to see. if you use iretryanalyzer , take the screenshot in ontestskipped too. what else to capture, and why it matters more than the image a screenshot alone often shows a normal-looking page. the context is what closes the bug. on failure, log: the url , driver.getcurrenturl() , because the test may have been on the wrong page entirely the browser and version , for a failure that only happens on firefox the data row , if it came from a @dataprovider the page source , when the element was missing rather than wrong the browser console logs , which catch the javascript error behind a blank page framework brief criterion 4 is exactly this: "a failure produces enough evidence to diagnose it without rerunning". a screenshot is one piece of that, not the whole of it. check yourself why must you copy the result of getscreenshotas(outputtype.file) ? the file is locked while the driver runs it is temporary and gets deleted the bytes are not written until copied why can a screenshot listener not read the driver field on your test class? the browser has already been quit by then listeners run on a separate thread entirely it only receives the result, not your object the screenshot itself throws inside the listener. what should you do? swallow it, and log that it failed rethrow it so nothing is hidden retry the screenshot three times you use iretryanalyzer and get no screenshots for retried attempts. why? the driver is quit before the retry runs those attempts fire ontestskipped instead retries are excluded from all listeners run it mvn test -dsurefire.suitexmlfiles=selenium.xml -dtest=screenshottest five tests, green, and a real .png lands in target/screenshots/ . then the part worth doing. open screenshottest.java , set fail_on_purpose to true , and rerun. one test fails, and the listener writes a second file: screenshot target/screenshots/screenshottest.thisonefails...-20260829-164835-309.png (url was file:///.../pages/lesson4.html) note what that failing test contains about screenshots: nothing. that is the whole point of the listener. set the constant back to false when you are done. primary source selenium's screenshots page, and the takesscreenshot javadoc , which is where the "temp file, copy it" warning comes from. files this lesson uses screenshottest.java , plus support/screenshotlistener.java and support/drivermanager.java , all new. five tests, verified green, and the listener verified by flipping the constant. where this connects testng lesson 7 for itestlistener and the retry gotcha. lesson 3 for why drivermanager is shaped the way it is. lesson 4 beat 4 is where you say all this out loud. ← lesson 7 the framework talk lesson 9 →
