s: You have run tests before. Today you write one, and hand the judging over to the machine.
x: lesson 1 · your first testng test lesson 01 · testng your first testng test you have run tests before. today you write one, and hand the judging over to the machine. the shift you are making every java program in this repo ends the same way. a main method prints something, and you read the output and decide whether it looked right. open palindrome.java and you will find exactly that. that works for three checks. it falls apart at three hundred, and it falls apart completely the moment someone else runs it, because the judgement lived in your head and nobody else has your head. a test framework moves the judgement into the code. testng does three jobs for you, and it is worth naming them separately because interviewers ask about them separately: it finds your test methods, so you never write main again. it runs them, in an order and a lifecycle you control. it judges them, and reports pass or fail without asking you. lesson 1 is only about the third job. the other two arrive in lessons 2 and 3. two words of vocabulary test method. an ordinary java method marked with @test . testng calls it. it must be public and it takes no arguments (until lesson 4, when data providers change that). assertion. a statement of what must be true. if it is true, nothing happens and the method keeps going. if it is false, it throws assertionerror and testng marks the test failed. that is the whole mechanism. a test passes by not throwing . the consequence people miss a test method with no assertion in it always passes. it cannot do anything else, because passing just means "did not throw". a test that prints and never asserts is theatre. write it create this file. type it rather than pasting it, this once. src/test/java/com/sdet/studyplan/testng/palindrometest.java package com.sdet.studyplan.testng; import com.sdet.studyplan.medium.palindrome; import org.testng.assert; import org.testng.annotations.test; // no main() method anywhere. that is the point. public class palindrometest { @test public void madamisapalindrome() { boolean result = palindrome.usingtwopointers( "madam" ); assert.asserttrue(result, "'madam' should be a palindrome" ); } @test public void helloisnotapalindrome() { boolean result = palindrome.usingtwopointers( "hello" ); assert.assertfalse(result, "'hello' should not be a palindrome" ); } } three details in that file are doing real work. the location. it sits under src/test/java , not src/main/java . maven treats those two trees differently: test code can see main code, main code cannot see test code, and test code is never packaged into the shipped jar. put a test in the wrong tree and it either will not run or will ship to production. the class name. palindrometest ends in test , and that is not a style choice. maven surefire, the plugin that runs tests during mvn test , only looks at classes matching test*.java , *test.java , *tests.java , or *testcase.java ( surefire docs ). name it palindromechecks and mvn test will report zero tests and a green build, which is the most dangerous output in this entire lesson. the second argument to the assertion. that message is what you will read at 2am when the build breaks. write it as a statement of what should be true, not a description of the code. run it mvn test -dtest=palindrometest -dtest= narrows the run to one class. drop it and maven runs every test in the project. you should see this: [info] t e s t s [info] ------------------------------------------------------- [info] running com.sdet.studyplan.testng.palindrometest [info] tests run: 2, failures: 0, errors: 0, skipped: 0, time elapsed: 0.164 s [info] [info] build success that is the win two methods you never called ran anyway, checked themselves, and reported. you wrote no main , no println , and no loop over test cases. testng found the methods by their annotation and did the rest. now break it on purpose this half matters more than the green run. a test you have never seen fail is a test you do not yet trust. change "hello" to "racecar" in the second method and run it again. [error] tests run: 2, failures: 1 , errors: 0, skipped: 0 <<< failure! [error] palindrometest.helloisnotapalindrome <<< failure! java.lang.assertionerror: 'hello' should not be a palindrome expected [false] but found [true] at org.testng.assert.assertfalse(assert.java:78) at ...palindrometest.helloisnotapalindrome( palindrometest.java:18 ) read that top line the way an interviewer would want you to. your message comes first, then testng's own expected [false] but found [true] , then the exact file and line. notice too that the first test still ran and still passed. one failure does not stop the suite. each test method stands alone. then put "hello" back and confirm it goes green again. the assertion methods, and the one that catches people everything lives in org.testng.assert , all static. the assertions you will actually use call fails when asserttrue(condition, msg) condition is false assertfalse(condition, msg) condition is true assertequals(actual, expected, msg) the two are not equal assertnotequals(actual, expected, msg) the two are equal assertnull(object, msg) object is not null assertnotnull(object, msg) object is null assertsame(actual, expected, msg) they are different objects in memory fail(msg) always — for branches that should be unreachable interview trap testng's order is assertequals(actual, expected) . junit's is the reverse, assertequals(expected, actual) . get it backwards and your test still works, but every failure message lies to you about which value was which. verified in the testng 7.7.0 source: public static void assertequals(object actual, object expected) . note that assertequals on objects uses .equals() , while assertsame compares references with == . that is the same distinction you met in palindrome.usingreverse . check yourself what does testng report for this method? @test public void checktotal() { system.out.println(2 + 2); } it fails, because nothing was asserted it is skipped, because there is nothing to check it passes, because nothing threw an error a class named loginchecks holds three @test methods. you run mvn test . what happens? all three test methods run and pass normally no tests run at all and the build is green the build fails with a class naming error you write assert.assertequals(5, list.size()) in testng, meaning "the size should be 5". what is the actual consequence? failure messages name the wrong value as actual the assertion silently passes whatever size is the test throws an argument order exception before the next lesson add one more test method to palindrometest that checks palindrome.usingreverse agrees with usingtwopointers on the word "racecar" . use assertequals and get the argument order right. then run the whole file and confirm three tests pass. lesson 2 takes on the second job: testng running your tests. that is the lifecycle annotations, @beforemethod through @aftersuite , and the execution order question that opens most sdet interviews. primary source read the introduction and "writing tests with testng" sections of the official testng documentation. ten minutes. it is written by the people who built it, and it is the source every claim above was checked against. stuck on anything? ask me. if a line in that file does not make sense, if the run does not look like the output above, or if you want to know why something is designed the way it is, say so and we will take it apart together. questions asked now are cheaper than questions asked in an interview. mission resources lesson 2 → the lifecycle annotations

s: TestNG's second job is running your tests. Ten annotations decide what happens around them, and one of them is named to mislead you.
x: lesson 2 · the lifecycle annotations lesson 02 · testng the lifecycle annotations testng's second job is running your tests. ten annotations decide what happens around them, and one of them is named to mislead you. the problem they solve in lesson 1 your tests needed no setup. real ones do. a selenium test opens a browser. a database test opens a connection. an api test fetches a token. put that work inside the test method and two things break: you repeat it in every test, and a failure in the setup gets reported as a test failure, which is a lie. so testng lets you hang setup and teardown code around your tests. the only real question is how wide a net each piece of setup should cast, and that is what the ten annotations are for. they are not ten different features. they are one feature at five different scopes. the five scopes the scopes nest, strictly, like boxes inside boxes. @beforesuite — the whole run @beforetest — one <test> tag in testng.xml @beforeclass — one java class @beforemethod — runs again for every test method @test read it from the outside in and you have the order the @before methods run. read it from the inside out and you have the order the @after methods run. there is no sixth rule to learn. everything else follows from the nesting. the fifth scope, @beforegroups and @aftergroups , hangs off group membership rather than off the boxes. park it until lesson 6. prove it yourself before you write anything, predict. two test methods, all ten annotations, one class. write down the order you expect on paper. then create this file. src/test/java/com/sdet/studyplan/testng/lifecycledemotest.java package com.sdet.studyplan.testng; import org.testng.annotations.*; public class lifecycledemotest { @beforesuite public void beforesuite() { system.out.println( "@beforesuite" ); } @beforetest public void beforetest() { system.out.println( "@beforetest" ); } @beforeclass public void beforeclass() { system.out.println( "@beforeclass" ); } @beforemethod public void beforemethod() { system.out.println( "@beforemethod" ); } @test public void testone() { system.out.println( " >>> testone" ); } @test public void testtwo() { system.out.println( " >>> testtwo" ); } @aftermethod public void aftermethod() { system.out.println( "@aftermethod" ); } @afterclass public void afterclass() { system.out.println( "@afterclass" ); } @aftertest public void aftertest() { system.out.println( "@aftertest" ); } @aftersuite public void aftersuite() { system.out.println( "@aftersuite" ); } } the import org.testng.annotations.*; is worth noticing. ten separate imports is noise, and this is the one place a wildcard import earns its keep. mvn test -dtest=lifecycledemotest @beforesuite @beforetest @beforeclass @beforemethod >>> testone @aftermethod @beforemethod >>> testtwo @aftermethod @afterclass @aftertest @aftersuite read the shape, not the list nine of those lines printed once. the @beforemethod and @aftermethod pair printed twice, once wrapped around each test. that is the only annotation pair that repeats, and it repeats because it is the innermost box. learn the shape and you never memorise the list. now the part that matters look again at that output. @beforesuite , @beforetest and @beforeclass all did the exact same thing: they printed once, in a row, at the start. with a single test class they are indistinguishable, which is precisely why people memorise the order and still get the concept wrong. add a second class and the difference appears. here is the real output from running two such classes together, class [a] and class [b] : [a] @beforesuite <- both classes' suite setup, up front [b] @beforesuite [a] @beforetest <- both classes' test setup, up front [b] @beforetest [b] @beforeclass <- class b's own setup, only now [b] @beforemethod [b] >>> testfour [b] @aftermethod [b] @beforemethod [b] >>> testthree [b] @aftermethod [b] @afterclass [a] @beforeclass <- class a's setup, after b has finished [a] @beforemethod [a] >>> testone [a] @aftermethod [a] @beforemethod [a] >>> testtwo [a] @aftermethod [a] @afterclass [a] @aftertest [b] @aftertest [a] @aftersuite [b] @aftersuite three things fall out of that, and all three are interview material. suite and test setup happen before any class starts. both classes' @beforesuite methods ran before either class did any work. suite scope means "before the whole run", not "before my class". class setup is bound to its own class. [a] @beforeclass waited until class b was completely finished. it fires immediately before the first test method of that class . class order is not alphabetical, and method order is not declaration order. b ran before a. testfour ran before testthree . testng makes no promise about either. if your tests need an order, you must ask for one, which is priority and dependsonmethods in lesson 5. if your tests need an order and you have not asked for one, you have a bug waiting for a slow day. the trap in the name @beforetest does not mean "before each @test ". that is @beforemethod . @beforetest means "before the classes inside one <test> tag in testng.xml " — the official wording is "run before any test method belonging to the classes inside the <test> tag is run" . the word "test" is doing two unrelated jobs in this framework. lesson 3 is entirely about the second job. what real code goes where interviewers ask this as "where would you launch the browser?". the answer is always the same trade: wider scope is faster, narrower scope is safer. choosing a scope annotation runs put this here @beforesuite once per run read config, start a driver server, open a db connection pool @beforetest once per <test> tag set up one browser or one environment that a whole group of classes shares @beforeclass once per class launch the browser, log in once for a group of related checks @beforemethod before every test method reset state, clear cookies, navigate back to a known page @aftermethod after every test method screenshot on failure, log out, clear test data @aftersuite once at the very end close the connection pool, write the summary report the honest default is @beforeclass to open the browser and @beforemethod to return it to a known state. opening a browser per method is correct but slow. opening one per suite is fast but lets one test poison every test after it. say that trade out loud in an interview and you sound like someone who has actually run a suite. check s: One test method, twenty rows of input, twenty results in the report. This is the most asked-about feature in TestNG interviews, and the half you already wrote months ago is the Excel half.
x: lesson 4 · @dataprovider and excel lesson 04 · testng @dataprovider, fed from an excel sheet one test method, twenty rows of input, twenty results in the report. this is the most asked-about feature in testng interviews, and the half you already wrote months ago is the excel half. the whole lesson in four lines 1. a @dataprovider is a method that returns rows of arguments. 2. a @test bound to one runs once per row , and each row gets its own pass or fail in the report. 3. the rows can come from anywhere, because it is just java. excel is the common source. 4. reading the sheet is apache poi's job, not testng's. keep the two apart. already in your repo datatable.readastable() in src/main/java/com/sdet/studyplan/excel/ turns a sheet into a list<map<string,string>> , one map per row keyed by the header names. you wrote it in july. its javadoc says "hand the list to a testng @dataprovider". this lesson is you cashing that in. why not just loop? the obvious move is a for loop inside one @test . it looks like it does the job. here are both approaches run against the same three words, with hello deliberately marked as a palindrome so one row must fail. a loop inside one @test checking madam checking hello (racecar never printed) tests run: 1, failures: 1 tmplooptest.allwords expected [true] but found [false] the same data as a @dataprovider tests run: 3, failures: 1 ispalindrome[hello, true](2) wrong verdict for 'hello' expected [true] but found [false] madam and racecar still ran three things the loop got wrong, and all three are the answer when an interviewer asks why data providers exist. the loop stopped at the first failure. a failed assertion throws, so racecar was never checked. you fix hello , rerun, and only then discover the next broken row. twenty rows means twenty round trips. the loop reported one result. "1 test, 1 failure" tells your manager nothing. the provider reported 3 tests and 1 failure, which is the true state of the system. the loop hid which input broke. look at the provider's failure name: ispalindrome[hello, true](2) . testng puts the row's arguments in the test name for free. no logging, no message building. the mechanism, with hardcoded rows learn it with no excel in the way. this file is already in your repo. src/test/java/com/sdet/studyplan/testng/dataproviderbasicstest.java public class dataproviderbasicstest { @dataprovider (name = "words" ) public object[][] words() { return new object[][] { { "madam" , true }, { "racecar" , true }, { "hello" , false }, { "madam" , false }, }; } @test (dataprovider = "words" ) public void ispalindrome(string word, boolean expected) { assert.assertequals(palindrome.usingtwopointers(word), expected, "wrong verdict for '" + word + "'" ); } } mvn test -dtest=dataproviderbasicstest tests run: 4 , failures: 0, errors: 0, skipped: 0 one @test method in the file. four results. that is the whole idea. madam with a capital m is in there on purpose. your usingtwopointers compares characters directly, so case matters, and the sheet records that as expected behaviour rather than leaving it undiscovered. the contract what testng requires of a provider rule detail return type object[][] , or iterator<object[]> for large or lazily-read data outer array one element per test run. four inner arrays means four runs inner array the arguments for one run, in parameter order method signature the @test parameters must match the inner array in count and type the name @dataprovider(name = "x") and @test(dataprovider = "x") must agree. omit name and it defaults to the method name where it lives same class by default. elsewhere with @test(dataprovider = "x", dataproviderclass = testdata.class) , which is how real frameworks share one provider across many tests exceptions it may declare throws . useful, since reading a file does the error you will hit first get the parameter count or type wrong and testng fails the test before your code runs, with a message about the data provider not matching the method signature. it is not a compile error, because the wiring happens by reflection at runtime. read the message and count the columns. now from excel step 1 the sheet testdata/palindrome-data.xlsx is in your repo. two columns, seven data rows. open it in excel and it looks like this: testdata/palindrome-data.xlsx, sheet "words" word expected why it is there madam true the happy case racecar true odd length hello false the negative case madam false case sensitivity, recorded on purpose (blank) true empty string, an edge case people forget a true single character 12321 true a numeric cell. this one is a trap, s: Which test runs first, what happens to the rest when one breaks, and the five @Test attributes that control a single method. Short lesson, heavy on interview questions.
x: lesson 5 · controlling execution lesson 05 · testng controlling execution which test runs first, what happens to the rest when one breaks, and the five @test attributes that control a single method. short lesson, heavy on interview questions. the whole lesson in four lines 1. priority decides order . it protects nothing. 2. dependsonmethods decides whether a test runs at all . a failed prerequisite means the dependent is skipped , not failed. 3. skipped and failed are different verdicts, and knowing why is the interview question. 4. timeout , expectedexceptions , enabled and invocationcount each control one method. two files in your repo run everything below: executionordertest.java and testattributestest.java . two problems that look like one lesson 2 showed that testng makes no promise about method order. sooner or later that hurts, and people reach for priority to fix it. half the time they have the wrong tool, because there are two separate problems here. ordering. run the smoke check before the long one. nothing breaks if you get it wrong, the report just reads oddly. that is priority . protection. do not attempt the checkout test if login failed, because a checkout failure caused by a broken login is a lie in your report. that is dependsonmethods . use the ordering tool for the protection job and you get a report full of failures that all trace back to one real bug. priority @test (priority = -5) public void runsfirst() { ... } @test public void nopriority() { ... } defaults to 0 @test (priority = 3) public void runslast() { ... } lower numbers first. negatives are legal and useful, because they let you push a method ahead of the default without renumbering everything else. two methods with the same priority run in an order testng does not define, so never rely on a tie. the part nobody mentions priority sorts methods within a class . it does not interleave across classes. i ran two classes inside one <test> tag, with priorities deliberately crossing over: priority -5 class a, all of it first no priority (0) priority 1 priority 3 [b] priority 0 class b, only now [b] priority 2 class b's priority 0 did not jump ahead of class a's priority 3 . class order comes from the order you list them in testng.xml , which testng honours because preserve-order defaults to true. i reversed the two lines in the xml and the whole output flipped. so: xml decides class order, priority decides method order inside each class. priority protects nothing this is the trap. a lower-priority method that fails does not stop the ones after it: priorityfirstfails failed priorityrunsanyway <-- still ran which is correct behaviour. priority is a sort key, nothing more. if you wanted the second one held back, you wanted a dependency. dependsonmethods flip break_login to true at the top of executionordertest.java and rerun. same seven tests, both times. break_login = false priority -5 login addtocart checkout cleanupanyway (alwaysrun) no priority (0) priority 3 tests run: 7 failures: 0, skipped: 0 break_login = true priority -5 login addtocart never ran checkout never ran cleanupanyway (alwaysrun) no priority (0) priority 3 tests run: 7 failures: 1, skipped: 2 one real failure. two skips. checkout depends on addtocart , which depends on login , so the whole chain came down from one broken link. why skipped and not failed a skipped test never ran . it has proven nothing, good or bad. reporting it as a failure would claim you found three bugs when you found one. this is the answer interviewers want, and it is why testng-failed.xml from lesson 3 contains skipped tests alongside failed ones: both still need proving. alwaysrun cleanupanyway also depends on login , and it ran in both columns: @test (dependsonmethods = "login" , alwaysrun = true ) public void cleanupanyway() { ... } alwaysrun = true turns a hard dependency into a soft one: keep the ordering, drop the skipping. it is for teardown-ish work that has to happen whether the prerequisite worked or not. the same attribute on a @before or @after method makes the configuration run even when its group is skipped. a dependency beats a priority give a dependent method an earlier priority than the thing it depends on and testng ignores the priority: @test (priority = 5) prerequisite() @test (priority = 1, dependsonmethods = "prerequisite" ) dependent() prerequisite (priority 5) ran first anyway dependent (priority 1) dependencies are a constraint. priority is a preference. constraints win. dependsongroups dependsonmethods names methods and breaks when you rename one. dependsongroups names groups instead, which survives refactoring and scales past a handful of methods: @test (groups = "auth" ) public void login() { ... } @test (groups = "auth" ) public void tokenrefresh() { ... } @test (dependsongroups = "auth" ) public void checkout() { ... } now checkout waits for everything tagged auth , wherever it lives, even in another class. groups are lesson 6. the @test attributes testattributestest.java has one of each, and the whole class passes. run it: mvn test -dtest=testattributestest finishesintime runsthreetimes runsthreetimes runsthreetimes tests run: 6 , failures: 0, errors: 0, skipped: 0 six results from five methods, and one of the five never ran at all. work out why before reading on. what each attribute does attribute effect use it for timeout = 500 fails the method if it runs past 500ms anything that can hang: a wait, an api call, a locator that never resolves expectedexceptions = x.class passes only if x is thrown testing that bad input is rejected expectedexceptionsmessageregexp the message must match too making sure it failed for the right reason enabled = false not run, and not counted anywhere quarantining a test. always leave the ticket number next to it invocationcount = 3 runs the method three times smoking out flakiness. pair with threadpoolsize for concurrency description = "..." text in the report saying what the test proves, in the report your manager reads so: five methods, one disabled, one invoked three times. 4 + 3 − 1 = 6. enabled = false does not show up as a skip. it vanishes. what the failures look like both of these are worth recognising on sight, because the message tells you exactly which attribute you tripped. timeout exceeded threadtimeoutexception: method ...tooslow() didn't finish within the time-out 300 expected exception never thrown method ...expectsbutnothing thrown() should have thrown an exception of type class java.lang.illegalstateexception expectedexceptions is blunt it passes if the exception is thrown anywhere in the method, including from your setup lines before you reach the call you meant to test. when the exact line matters, use a try/catch with an assert.fail() after the call, or assert.assertthrows(x.class, () -> ...) , which scopes the expectation to one lambda. should tests depend on each other at all? mostly no, and saying so is worth more than reciting the syntax. dependencies make tests non-independent. you can no longer run one in isolation, the order is fixed so you lose parallelism across the chain, and one flaky prerequisite turns green tests yellow. the usual reason people reach for dependsonmethods is that test two needs state that test one created, and the better fix for that is a @beforemethod that creates the state directly. the legitimate uses are narrow and worth naming, because that is the answer that sounds experienced: a login or token call that two hundred later tests need, where running them all against a dead session wastes twenty minutes and produces two hundred misleading failures an environment health check that gates the suite genuinely sequential workflows, where "add to cart" without "search" is not a test of anything the one-sentence version for an interview: i use dependsonmethods for real prerequisites like auth, so a broken login reports as one failure and two hundred skips instead of two hundred failures, and i avoid it everywhere else because it costs test independence. check yourself method a has priority = 1 and fails. method b has priority = 2 . what happens to b? it is skipped, a failed before it it runs normally it fails too, failures cascade login fails. addtocart depends on it, and checkout depends on addtocart . what does the report say? 3 failures 1 failure, 2 passes 1 failure, 2 skips dependent has priority = 1 and depends on prerequisite , which has priority = 5 . which runs first? prerequisite, the dependency wins dependent, the lower priority wins neither, testng reports a cycle what does alwaysrun = true do on a method that also has dependsonmethods ? removes the dependency completely keeps the order, stops the skipping reruns the method until it passes before the next lesson flip break_login to true , run executionordertest , and read the counts: failures: 1, skipped: 2 with it still broken, run mvn test -dsurefire.suitexmlfiles=target/surefire-reports/testng-failed.xml and confirm all three chain methods are in there, not just the one that failed flip it back add description = "..." to two tests, rerun, and find your text in target/surefire-reports/index.html that second step closes the loop with lesson 3. it is also the cleanest way to prove to yourself that skipped tests are treated as unproven rather than as passes. lesson 6 is groups and parallel execution: tagging tests as smoke or regression, filtering them from testng.xml , and the four values of the parallel attribute. it is where the <test> tag from lesson 3 finally pays off. primary source read dependencies and the @test attribute table in annotations . both are short. files this lesson uses executionordertest.java and testattributestest.java , both new in src/test/java/com/sdet/studyplan/testng/ . both pass as shipped. stuck on anything? ask me. worth asking: "what happens if two tests depend on each other?" testng detects the cycle and the error message is not obvious the first time you see it. ← lesson 4 mission lesson 6 → groups and parallel

(alwaysrun) no priority (0) priority 3 tests run: 7 failures: 0, skipped: 0 break_login = true priority -5 login addtocart never ran checkout never ran cleanupanyway (alwaysrun) no priority (0) priority 3 tests run: 7 failures: 1, skipped: 2 one real failure. two skips. checkout depends on addtocart , which depends on login , so the whole chain came down from one broken link. why skipped and not failed a skipped test never ran . it has proven nothing, good or bad. reporting it as a failure would claim you found three bugs when you found one. this is the answer interviewers want, and it is why testng-failed.xml from lesson 3 contains skipped tests alongside failed ones: both still need proving. alwaysrun cleanupanyway also depends on login , and it ran in both columns: @test (dependsonmethods = "login" , alwaysrun = true ) public void cleanupanyway() { ... } alwaysrun = true turns a hard dependency into a soft one: keep the ordering, drop the skipping. it is for teardown-ish work that has to happen whether the prerequisite worked or not. the same attribute on a @before or @after method makes the configuration run even when its group is skipped. a dependency beats a priority give a dependent method an earlier priority than the thing it depends on and testng ignores the priority: @test (priority = 5) prerequisite() @test (priority = 1, dependsonmethods = "prerequisite" ) dependent() prerequisite (priority 5) ran first anyway dependent (priority 1) dependencies are a constraint. priority is a preference. constraints win. dependsongroups dependsonmethods names methods and breaks when you rename one. dependsongroups names groups instead, which survives refactoring and scales past a handful of methods: @test (groups = "auth" ) public void login() { ... } @test (groups = "auth" ) public void tokenrefresh() { ... } @test (dependsongroups = "auth" ) public void checkout() { ... } now checkout waits for everything tagged auth , wherever it lives, even in another class. groups are lesson 6.

the @test attributes testattributestest.java has one of each, and the whole class passes. run it: mvn test -dtest=testattributestest finishesintime runsthreetimes runsthreetimes runsthreetimes tests run: 6 , failures: 0, errors: 0, skipped: 0 six results from five methods, and one of the five never ran at all. work out why before reading on. what each attribute does attribute effect use it for timeout = 500 fails the method if it runs past 500ms anything that can hang: a wait, an api call, a locator that never resolves expectedexceptions = x.class passes only if x is thrown testing that bad input is rejected expectedexceptionsmessageregexp the message must match too making sure it failed for the right reason enabled = false not run, and not counted anywhere quarantining a test. always leave the ticket number next to it invocationcount = 3 runs the method three times smoking out flakiness. pair with threadpoolsize for concurrency description = "..." text in the report saying what the test proves, in the report your manager reads so: five methods, one disabled, one invoked three times. 4 + 3 − 1 = 6. enabled = false does not show up as a skip. it vanishes. what the failures look like both of these are worth recognising on sight, because the message tells you exactly which attribute you tripped. timeout exceeded threadtimeoutexception: method ...tooslow() didn't finish within the time-out 300 expected exception never thrown method ...expectsbutnothing thrown() should have thrown an exception of type class java.lang.illegalstateexception expectedexceptions is blunt it passes if the exception is thrown anywhere in the method, including from your setup lines before you reach the call you meant to test. when the exact line matters, use a try/catch with an assert.fail() after the call, or assert.assertthrows(x.class, () -> ...) , which scopes the expectation to one lambda.

t: Should tests depend on each other at all?
x: should tests depend on each other at all? mostly no, and saying so is worth more than reciting the syntax. dependencies make tests non-independent. you can no longer run one in isolation, the order is fixed so you lose parallelism across the chain, and one flaky prerequisite turns green tests yellow. the usual reason people reach for dependsonmethods is that test two needs state that test one created, and the better fix for that is a @beforemethod that creates the state directly. the legitimate uses are narrow and worth naming, because that is the answer that sounds experienced: a login or token call that two hundred later tests need, where running them all against a dead session wastes twenty minutes and produces two hundred misleading failures an environment health check that gates the suite genuinely sequential workflows, where "add to cart" without "search" is not a test of anything the one-sentence version for an interview: i use dependsonmethods for real prerequisites like auth, so a broken login reports as one failure and two hundred skips instead of two hundred failures, and i avoid it everywhere else because it costs test independence.

check yourself method a has priority = 1 and fails. method b has priority = 2 . what happens to b? it is skipped, a failed before it it runs normally it fails too, failures cascade login fails. addtocart depends on it, and checkout depends on addtocart . what does the report say? 3 failures 1 failure, 2 passes 1 failure, 2 skips dependent has priority = 1 and depends on prerequisite , which has priority = 5 . which runs first? prerequisite, the dependency wins dependent, the lower priority wins neither, testng reports a cycle what does alwaysrun = true do on a method that also has dependsonmethods ? removes the dependency completely keeps the order, stops the skipping reruns the method until it passes

before the next lesson flip break_login to true , run executionordertest , and read the counts: failures: 1, skipped: 2 with it still broken, run mvn test -dsurefire.suitexmlfiles=target/surefire-reports/testng-failed.xml and confirm all three chain methods are in there, not just the one that failed flip it back add description = "..." to two tests, rerun, and find your text in target/surefire-reports/index.html that second step closes the loop with lesson 3. it is also the cleanest way to prove to yourself that skipped tests are treated as unproven rather than as passes. lesson 6 is groups and parallel execution: tagging tests as smoke or regression, filtering them from testng.xml , and the four values of the parallel attribute. it is where the <test> tag from lesson 3 finally pays off. primary source read dependencies and the @test attribute table in annotations . both are short. files this lesson uses executionordertest.java and testattributestest.java , both new in src/test/java/com/sdet/studyplan/testng/ . both pass as shipped. stuck on anything? ask me. worth asking: "what happens if two tests depend on each other?" testng detects the cycle and the error message is not obvious the first time you see it. ← lesson 4 mission lesson 6 → groups and parallel

p: Lesson 7 · Listeners, reports, and the talk
x: what a listener is for you want a screenshot on every failure. you could put a try/catch in all four hundred tests. nobody does that. instead you write one class that testng calls at every interesting moment, and the tests stay ignorant of it. itestlistener is the one you will use. six methods, and the names say what they do: itestlistener method fires real use onstart before a <test> tag start a report, note the environment onteststart before each test method log the name, start a timer ontestsuccess after a pass mark it green in a custom report ontestfailure after a fail screenshot , page source, browser console log ontestskipped after a skip record why it never ran onfinish after the tag close the report, print totals, email it logginglistener.java in your repo implements all six. there is no browser in this project, so instead of a screenshot its ontestfailure appends to target/test-failures.log . same hook, same idea, an artifact you can open afterwards. @override public void ontestfailure(itestresult result) { system.out.println( "l> fail " + result.getname()); // in a selenium framework this line is the screenshot instead write(localtime.now() + " " + result.gettestclass().getname() + "." + result.getname() + " -> " + result.getthrowable().getmessage()); } flip demo_failure to true in listenerdemotest.java , rerun, and the file appears: 14:02:37 com.sdet.studyplan.testng.listenerdemotest.failsonpurpose -> deliberate failure for the listener demo expected [false] but found [true] itestresult is the thing worth knowing. it carries the method name, the class, the throwable, the parameters from your lesson 4 data provider, timings, and the itestcontext . everything a report needs comes off that object. three ways to register one how scope when @listeners(logginglistener.class) on a class that class quick, and fine for a demo <listeners> in testng.xml the whole suite the normal choice. one place, no test touched meta-inf/services/org.testng.itestnglistener everything on the classpath shipping a listener inside a shared jar listeners.xml uses the middle one: <suite name="listenerdemo" > <listeners> <listener class-name="com.sdet.studyplan.testng.logginglistener" /> </listeners> ... the other interfaces exist and are worth being able to name: isuitelistener wraps the whole suite rather than a tag, iinvokedmethodlistener fires around configuration methods too, and ireporter runs once at the very end with the complete results, which is what report libraries hook into.
